title: Fix data integrity first, then account structure, then creative
hypothesis: If we fix data integrity first, then account structure, then creative, then every later call moves faster because it is judged on data that is now trustworthy.

signal.check: An audit or restructure is starting and nobody has confirmed order data and margin data are trustworthy yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources rank data as fastest to fix and creative as slowest but largest impact

risk.note: Reordering work, not changing the account.

prerequisites: Access to order data with a new vs returning flag
Access to the Meta or TikTok ad account
steps: List every open issue: data gaps, structure problems, weak creative.
Fix data and tracking gaps first, since they are fast and everything else depends on them.
Fix account and campaign structure second.
Brief new creative last, since it is the slowest fix to pay off.

test.method: Track how long each fix took and whether later reads changed once data was fixed.
test.read_point: After the data fixes are live, before judging structure or creative.

title: Score every account structure on a readable-data test and a commercial-alignment test
hypothesis: If every account structure must pass a readable-data test and a commercial-alignment test, then bad structures get caught early because failing either test forces a rebuild before money is wasted.

signal.check: Nobody can say whether the current structure supports a weekly read-decide-wait loop, or whether budget can flex to the categories and regions the business needs.

risk.note: A review, not a change, until it flags a rebuild.

prerequisites: List of current campaigns and ad sets with targeting
steps: Write down whether you can read a decision, wait, and decide again on this structure.
Write down whether budget can flex to the categories, ranges, regions and personas the business needs.
Check that no low-margin line can absorb spend without anyone seeing it.
If either check fails, plan a restructure.

test.method: Score the structure yes or no on both tests and log the date.
test.read_point: Immediately, then again after any restructure.

title: Confirm unit economics before setting any scale plan
hypothesis: If we review first-order AOV, gross margin and 365-day LTV before setting a scale plan, then the scale ceiling stays realistic because tactics cannot out-earn bad unit economics.

signal.check: A scale-up or a higher CPA target is being discussed before anyone has confirmed AOV, gross margin and LTV payback for the SKU or store.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources say economics set the ceiling that tactics cannot beat

risk.note: Wrong economics data leads to a scale plan that loses money.

prerequisites: AOV, gross margin and 365-day LTV by product or category
steps: Pull first-order AOV and gross margin by category, monthly.
Pull 365-day LTV or a repeat-rate proxy for the same categories.
Set the sustainable bid as first-order gross profit plus what retention can add.
Only after this, approve or raise a scale plan or CPA target.

test.method: Compare the planned CPA target against the sustainable bid built from margin and LTV.
test.read_point: Before any budget increase is approved.

title: Reconcile platform ROAS against acquisition MER before any keep, kill or scale call
hypothesis: If we compare platform ROAS to acquisition MER before every keep, kill or scale call, then we stop acting on inflated numbers because a wide gap flags existing-customer credit or view-through inflation.

signal.check: Keep, kill or scale decisions are made from platform ROAS alone, with no acquisition MER or store period ROAS calculated alongside it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; example gap in sources is 3x to 7x aMER versus 17x platform ROAS

risk.note: A reporting check, not an account change.

prerequisites: Store orders split new vs returning
Ad spend by platform
steps: Calculate acquisition MER: new-customer revenue divided by ad spend, monthly.
Put platform ROAS beside acquisition MER for the same period.
If platform ROAS is far above acquisition MER, suspect existing-customer credit or view-through attribution.
Do not approve a keep, kill or scale call until the two numbers are reconciled or the gap is explained.

test.method: Track the gap between platform ROAS and acquisition MER each month.

title: Test and log every Ads Manager suggestion before applying it
hypothesis: If every Ads Manager recommendation or opportunity score is tested and logged before being applied, then wasted changes drop because most platform-wide updates aim to raise Meta's take, not the store's ROAS.

signal.check: Ads Manager recommendations, opportunity score prompts, or projected uplift claims are being applied without a before-and-after test in this account's own data.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a profitable account can show opportunity score 0

risk.note: Skipping or testing a suggestion; no account change is forced.

steps: List every Ads Manager suggestion or prompt received this month.
For each, either skip it or test it on a small slice of budget with a before and after read.
Log the result next to the suggestion.
Never apply a suggestion on its projected uplift number alone.

test.method: Apply the suggestion on one ad set, leave a matched ad set untouched, compare CPA after 1 read window.

title: Plan a yearly creative and page refresh to offset CPM inflation
hypothesis: If we plan a yearly creative and landing-page improvement to offset roughly 20% to 30% CPM inflation, then last year's break-even offer keeps paying back because rising costs are met with rising performance.

signal.check: The account is running the same creative, offer and landing page as 12 months ago with no planned refresh, while CPMs have likely risen.

risk.note: A planning input, not an account change on its own.

prerequisites: Own CPM trend by year, if available
steps: Pull this account's own CPM by month for the last 12 to 24 months, if available.
Assume about 20% to 30% CPM inflation a year if no own data exists.
Plan a creative refresh and a landing-page conversion improvement for the year that offsets that rise.
Re-check the break-even math on offers that worked 12 months ago.

test.method: Compare this year's CPM to last year's CPM for the same audience and season.

title: Require a written one-line defendable purpose for every campaign
hypothesis: If every campaign must pass a one-line defendable purpose test, then wasted structure drops because campaigns kept only from habit get merged or cut.

signal.check: The account has more than one cold campaign and no written one-line purpose exists for each one.

expected_effect.size: many $1M to $5M a month accounts run only 4 or 5 campaigns

risk.note: A naming and merge exercise, not a targeting change.

prerequisites: List of all live campaigns with targeting and budget
steps: List every live campaign.
Write a one-line purpose for each: different margin, non-overlapping persona, own region, promo cadence, or a funnel big enough to KPI alone.
Flag any campaign whose only purpose is spend feels big or duplicates another cold campaign.
Merge or cut flagged campaigns.

test.method: Count campaigns before and after, and check performance held on the surviving structure.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after any merge.

title: Merge campaigns whose conversion volume is too thin to optimise well
hypothesis: If we merge campaigns until each holds well above 100 conversions a month, then each campaign's optimisation improves because it is no longer learning on a thin, split data set.

signal.check: Total account conversions divided by number of cold campaigns is well under 100 to 200 a month per campaign.

expected_effect.size: about a 5% to 10% efficiency swing from splitting at ad set level instead of campaign level

risk.note: Merging campaigns changes reporting history; keep old names logged.

prerequisites: Monthly conversions per campaign
steps: Pull monthly conversions for each cold campaign.
Divide total conversions by number of campaigns.
If well under 100 to 200 per campaign, merge campaigns that share a commercial reason.
Move any variable you still want to learn, like creative concept, to ad set level instead of campaign level.

test.method: Compare CPA and conversion rate before and after merging, over one full read window.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the merge.

title: Only fully consolidate into one campaign for a single product, single persona, small-spend store
hypothesis: If full consolidation into one campaign is reserved for single-product, single-persona, small-spend stores, then wasted spend drops because complex stores stop hiding margin and persona differences inside one learning pool.

signal.check: The account runs one Advantage+ or fully consolidated campaign while selling multiple categories, margins or personas.

expected_effect.size: about 90% of brands are wrong to fully consolidate

risk.note: Splitting a working consolidated campaign can reset learning; do it as a planned test.

prerequisites: Margin, persona and audience overlap by category
steps: List categories or ranges by margin, persona and region.
Check for margin spread, non-overlapping audiences, or very high AOV with low conversion volume.
If any of these hold, segment into business-unit campaigns with concept ad sets instead of one campaign.
Keep full consolidation only for single product, single persona, small spend.

test.method: Split the consolidated campaign into segmented campaigns and compare margin-weighted ROAS after one read window.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the split.

title: Use the small-spend template: one testing campaign, optional scaling, optional small retention campaign
hypothesis: If a small-spend account runs one testing campaign of concept ad sets plus an optional scaling campaign, then structure stops being the bottleneck because the default matches its low conversion volume.

signal.check: Monthly Meta spend is under about $50,000 and the account runs a more complex structure than a testing campaign and an optional scaling campaign.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this is a safe default, not a guaranteed lift

risk.note: A structure rebuild; keep the old structure live until the new one has one full read window.

prerequisites: Monthly spend by platform
steps: Confirm monthly Meta spend is under about $50,000.
Build one testing campaign with concept ad sets of 3 to 5 ads each.
Add an optional scaling campaign only once a winner is confirmed.
Add a small existing-customer campaign only if repeat purchase is expected.
Exclude existing customers from testing and scaling; set attribution to 7-day click; never read under 5 days.

test.method: Run the template for one read cycle and compare CPA and structure clarity against the prior structure.

title: Use the mid-spend template: 2 to 3 cold campaigns with a stated reason, higher ad volume
hypothesis: If a $50k to $250k a month account runs 2 to 3 cold campaigns split by a real commercial reason, with 100 to 300 new ads a month, then structure supports growth because the split matches funnel, persona or category differences.
does_not_apply_when: Monthly Meta spend under about $50,000 or above about $250,000

signal.check: Monthly spend is in the $50k to $250k range and the account runs either one giant campaign or many campaigns with no clear commercial split.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this template is a starting point

risk.note: Splitting into more campaigns changes learning; roll out gradually.

prerequisites: Monthly spend, LTV and repeat rate by category if available
steps: Confirm monthly spend is in the $50k to $250k range.
Split into 2 or 3 cold campaigns only where funnel, persona or landing pages genuinely differ.
Build concept ad sets inside each campaign.
Target 100 to 300 new ads a month across the account.

test.method: Compare CPA and creative throughput before and after the split, over one full read window.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the rebuild.

title: Use the large-spend template: mandatory page strategy and bidding diversity across campaigns
hypothesis: If a $250k or more a month account runs a page strategy and bids differently across campaigns, then the account stops hitting ad and page limits because volume is spread instead of stacked in one place.

signal.check: Monthly spend is above about $250,000 and the account has no page strategy or every campaign uses the same bid logic.

risk.note: Adding pages and bid diversity does not remove existing campaigns.

prerequisites: Monthly spend at or above about $250,000
steps: Confirm monthly spend is above about $250,000.
Build extra duplicate brand pages, partnership pages or regional pages ahead of the live-ad cap.
Vary bid strategy across campaigns instead of using the same setting everywhere.
Keep testing volume up even at this spend level.

test.method: Track live ads per page and CPA spread across campaigns after adding pages and bid diversity.

title: Open a second ad account on the same pixel once spend passes about $250k a month
hypothesis: If we open a second ad account on the same pixel with different bid logic once spend passes about $250,000 a month, then account risk drops because a ban or billing failure on the main account no longer stops all delivery.
does_not_apply_when: Splitting by country for reasons other than billing currency

signal.check: Monthly spend is above about $250,000 and every ad runs through a single ad account with no fallback.

expected_effect.size: second account might hold about 10% of spend

risk.note: Setting up and syncing a second account takes real work to reverse cleanly.

prerequisites: Monthly spend above about $250,000
Shared pixel access
steps: Confirm the pixel can be shared across two ad accounts.
Open a second ad account under the same Business Manager.
Give it a different bid logic, such as maximise value or cost caps, from the main account.
Route about 10% of spend through it as a fallback, and use it if the main account is banned or billing fails.

test.method: Run the second account for one read window and compare its CPA to the main account's CPA on the same offers.

title: Split campaigns by business unit, ad sets by concept, never by launch date
hypothesis: If campaign splits follow business units and ad set splits follow the creative concept, with no launch-date batches, then performance stays readable because each layer answers one clear question.

signal.check: Ad sets are named or grouped by launch date, format splits exist above small new-account spend, or many low-budget campaigns exist for categories that could be ad sets.

risk.note: A regrouping exercise on existing ads and ad sets.

prerequisites: List of ad sets with current names and split logic
steps: Check whether any campaigns are split by category when an ad set split would work instead.
Check whether any ad sets are split by launch date, format, or landing page outside a real test.
Rebuild splits so campaigns follow business units and ad sets follow the creative concept.
Rename and re-group without deleting history.

test.method: Compare CPA readability and decision speed before and after the regroup.

title: Run recurring promos in their own campaign
hypothesis: If recurring promos on about a 3 to 4 week cadence run in their own campaign, then testing and scaling data stays clean because price-sensitive promo traffic no longer mixes into evergreen concept learning.

signal.check: A promo runs every 3 to 4 weeks or on any recurring cadence inside the same campaigns used for testing and scaling.

risk.note: Splitting a promo out does not change the offer itself.

prerequisites: A recurring promo calendar
steps: Identify any promo that recurs on a set cadence.
Build a separate campaign for it.
Keep testing and scaling campaigns running promo-free in between.
Compare learning stability in the evergreen campaigns after the split.

test.method: Compare evergreen campaign CPA stability before and after moving promos to their own campaign.

title: Spin a funnel into its own campaign once it is big enough to KPI alone
hypothesis: If a funnel such as advertorials is pulled into its own campaign once it nears about 30% of total spend, then that funnel gets judged fairly because it is no longer blended into a campaign built for a different funnel.

signal.check: One funnel or format, such as advertorials, is approaching or has passed about 30% of total spend while still living inside the general testing structure.

risk.note: Moving a funnel to its own campaign is a structural change, not a spend change.

prerequisites: Spend share by funnel or format
steps: Track spend share by funnel or format monthly.
When one funnel nears about 30% of total spend, plan a dedicated campaign for it.
Move that funnel's ad sets into the new campaign.
Keep the smaller structure inside the general testing campaign for everything else.

test.method: Compare that funnel's CPA before and after it gets its own campaign.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the move.

title: Fix reporting problems with naming and filters, not new campaigns
hypothesis: If reporting problems get solved with naming conventions and saved filters instead of new campaigns, then account structure stays simple because structure is reserved for real learning splits, not tidiness.

signal.check: A new campaign is being proposed and the only reason given is cleaner reporting, easier filtering, or international grouping.

risk.note: Refusing a structure change; no account risk.

prerequisites: Consistent naming convention already agreed
steps: Ask what the new campaign would let the account learn that it cannot learn now.
If the answer is only cleaner reporting, reject the new campaign.
Fix the reporting problem with naming conventions and saved filters instead.
Reserve new campaigns for a real commercial or learning reason.

test.method: Track the number of campaigns added for reporting reasons over a quarter after adopting this rule.

title: Ramp budget and structure ahead of a peak sale and fix a wind-down date before it starts
hypothesis: If we ramp budget and structure ahead of a peak sale event and fix a wind-down date before it starts, then peak spend stops overrunning the sale window because a plan, not momentum, decides when it ends.

signal.check: A peak sale event like a major shopping festival is coming and there is no written ramp date, sale-specific ad set, or wind-down date yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; CPM tends to inflate in a cycle around peak sale periods

risk.note: No source in this folder gives a tested ramp or wind-down procedure; verify against the brand's own past sale performance.

prerequisites: A sale calendar
Past sale performance data if available
steps: Set a ramp start date ahead of the sale.
Build or flag sale-price ad sets or campaigns separate from evergreen ones.
Plan pre-sale creative and audience warm-up.
Fix a wind-down date and budget step-down before the sale starts.

test.method: Compare CPM and CAC during the ramp, peak and wind-down windows against the same sale last year, if available.

title: Give cross-border buyers their own currency, delivery time and duty messaging
hypothesis: If cross-border buyers see their own currency, delivery time and duty messaging instead of the domestic version, then conversion improves because the page stops assuming a shopper who is not there.
does_not_apply_when: Store sells into only one currency zone or country

signal.check: The store sells into a second currency zone or country and the ad or landing page still shows domestic currency, delivery time or duty terms.

risk.note: A messaging and display change, not a pricing change.

prerequisites: Confirmed second currency zone or country with real order volume
steps: List every country or currency zone with meaningful cross-border orders.
Add local currency display for each.
Add accurate delivery time and duty or customs messaging for each.
Route ads for that country to the matching page version.

test.method: Compare conversion rate for cross-border traffic before and after adding local currency and delivery messaging.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the page change.

title: Define a concept as SKU, pain point and offer; change any one and start a new ad set
hypothesis: If a concept is fixed as the SKU, the buyer's pain or occasion, and the offer, and any change starts a new ad set, then reads stay clean because two different concepts never share one learning pool.

signal.check: Ad sets mix more than one SKU, pain point or offer under a single name, or a changed offer stays in the same ad set as the old one.

risk.note: A naming and grouping discipline, not a targeting change.

prerequisites: A concept matrix of persona, angle and offer from the creative team
steps: Write each ad set's concept as SKU or range, stated pain or occasion, and offer.
Check that every ad inside an ad set shares the same three elements.
When any one element changes, build a new ad set instead of editing the old one.
Keep ad type or format flexible inside a concept.

test.method: Compare read clarity and CPA variance for ad sets before and after enforcing single-concept ad sets.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the cleanup.

title: Load each concept ad set with enough ads for 2 to 6 exposures before purchase, minimum 3
hypothesis: If each concept ad set carries at least 3 ads and up to 15, then the concept gets a fair read because shoppers typically need 2 to 6 exposures before they buy.

signal.check: A concept ad set runs with only 1 or 2 ads, or with 50 or more ads that likely span more than one concept.

expected_effect.size: unknown; min 3, typical 3 to 15, up to 20 for large reads

risk.note: Adding or trimming ads inside an existing ad set.

prerequisites: 3 or more distinct ads for the concept
steps: Count ads currently in each concept ad set.
If under 3, add more variations before judging the concept.
If well over 15 to 20, check whether the ad set actually spans more than one concept and split it.
Keep the ad count in the 3 to 15 range for most concepts.

test.method: Compare read reliability and CPA for ad sets moved into the 3 to 15 range.

title: Launch every new concept with the concept ad plus 3 hook variations
hypothesis: If a new concept launches with the core ad plus 3 hook variations, then a good concept is not killed for a single weak hook because at least one variation gets a fair read.

signal.check: A new concept is launched with only 1 ad and no hook variations.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source reports a hook variation winning while the original lost

risk.note: Adding creative variations, not changing the offer.

prerequisites: 3 or more hook variations of the concept ad
steps: Brief 3 hook variations alongside the core concept ad.
Launch all 4 together in the new concept's ad set.
Read them together at the test's read point, not individually before then.
Expect variations of an already-proven top ad to extend its life more often than beat it.

test.method: Compare kill rate on new concepts launched with 1 ad versus 4 ads including hook variations.
test.read_point: At the concept's first read date.

title: Keep non-overlapping personas out of the same ad set
hypothesis: If men's and women's or other non-overlapping personas never share an ad set, then delivery targets a real group because a mixed ad set has no single audience to optimise toward.

signal.check: One ad set targets two clearly different personas, such as a men's and a women's range, or the ad-level gender or age breakdown shows delivery split across unrelated groups.

risk.note: Splitting an ad set by persona is a structural change, not a targeting restriction.

prerequisites: A gender or age breakdown per ad
steps: Pull the gender or age breakdown per ad for mixed-audience ad sets.
If delivery splits unevenly across personas with no shared intent, split the ad set.
Build one ad set per persona with matching creative.
Re-check the breakdown after the split.

test.method: Compare CPA per persona before and after the split.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the split.

title: Group all funnel stages for one persona in one ad set, or blend the numbers before deciding if split by stage
hypothesis: If funnel-stage ad sets for one persona are either grouped together or blended back to the persona level before a decision, then stage splits stop causing bad kill calls because a 2x and 6x split misread as two failing ad sets is corrected to the true 4x blend.

signal.check: Top, middle and bottom funnel ads for the same persona sit in separate ad sets and are being judged separately without blending the numbers back together.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a consolidated 4x ad set split wrongly reads as 2x and 6x separately

risk.note: A reporting and grouping decision, not a spend change.

prerequisites: Ad sets tagged by funnel stage and persona
steps: Decide whether to group all stages for a persona in one ad set, or split by stage as separate concepts.
If split by stage, always blend the numbers back to the persona level before any kill or scale call.
Never judge a stage-split ad set in isolation.
Document which approach the account uses so future reads stay consistent.

test.method: Compare kill and scale decisions made on blended versus unblended stage-split data.
test.read_point: At every read point for stage-split ad sets.

title: Name every ad set with persona, angle, offer, content type and launch date, never a batch name
hypothesis: If every ad set is named with persona, angle, offer, content type and launch date instead of a batch label, then anyone can audit the account because the name always matches what it actually targets.

signal.check: Ad sets are named with vague batch labels like a date range, or names do not describe persona, angle or offer.

risk.note: A rename, not a targeting or budget change.

prerequisites: Agreed naming convention for the account
steps: Write the naming convention: persona, angle, offer, content type, launch date.
Rename every current ad set and campaign to match, including old ones when taking over an account.
Apply the same convention on TikTok as product plus objective plus date at campaign level.
Check new ad sets follow the convention before they launch.

test.method: Audit a sample of ad set names monthly against the convention.

title: Never touch a winning ad set; fork new creative into a new ad set beside it
hypothesis: If new creative for a winning concept always launches in a new ad set beside the winner, then the winner keeps hitting KPI because it is never disturbed by an untested addition.

signal.check: New creative is being added directly into an ad set that is already hitting KPI, instead of into a new forked ad set.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source calls this the number 1 rule of Meta buying

risk.note: Expect ad-set sprawl: several ad sets may belong to one winning concept.

prerequisites: A confirmed winning ad set at KPI
steps: Check whether the target ad set is currently hitting KPI.
If it is, build a new ad set with the same concept fields plus the new creative.
If it is missing KPI, add the new ads directly into it instead.
Name the fork with the same concept fields plus the new launch date.

test.method: Track whether winning ad sets stay at KPI after adopting the fork rule versus before.

title: Go broad in cold targeting and let the product page, price and reviews qualify the buyer
hypothesis: If cold campaigns target broad with only hard controls, then delivery finds real buyers because the product page, price and reviews do the qualifying that interest targeting used to attempt.

signal.check: Cold campaigns still use interest stacks, lookalikes, or narrow age and gender bands as the main targeting method.

risk.note: Removing interests can feel risky; test broad on a new ad set rather than editing a live winner.

prerequisites: A product page, price and reviews that already qualify the buyer
steps: Remove interest, lookalike and narrow age or gender targeting from new cold ad sets.
Keep only hard controls: exclusions, minimum age, locations and languages.
Let the creative and landing page carry the audience signal instead.
Compare results against the narrower version if one is running.

test.method: Run a broad ad set beside a matched interest-targeted ad set with the same creative for one read window.

title: Cap any interest, lookalike or custom audience test as a small sandbox
hypothesis: If interest, lookalike or custom audience tests run only inside a small capped sandbox, then a brand that wants to keep testing them does so without risking the account's main broad budget.

signal.check: Interest, lookalike or custom audience ad sets are running with no stated spend cap or end date.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no cap amount given by source, so use the account's own test-sizing rule

risk.note: A budget-cap decision, not removing the audience type.

prerequisites: A test-sizing method already in place (see test-sizing ideas)
steps: Decide a small fixed budget cap for any interest, lookalike or custom audience test.
Set an end date or spend threshold before launch.
Spend the time saved from not managing a bigger sandbox on more creative instead.
Review the sandbox result against a matched broad ad set.

test.method: Compare CPA of the capped sandbox against a matched broad ad set over the same window.

title: Put the target audience in the creative and copy, not in the targeting settings
hypothesis: If the audience is defined through casting, hook, copy and landing page instead of targeting settings, then broad delivery still reaches the right buyer because the ad itself does the qualifying.

signal.check: Targeting is broad but the creative gives no clear signal of who it is for through casting, hook, copy or landing page match.

risk.note: Identity words in copy must not misstate the offer or break personal-attribute ad policy; check current policy before using them.

prerequisites: Broad targeting already in place
steps: Cast the age and gender of people shown in the ad to match the intended buyer.
Write hooks, headlines and copy that speak clearly to that buyer's situation.
Match the landing page to the same buyer signal.
Check personal-attribute ad policy before naming the buyer directly in copy, such as identity words in a headline.

test.method: Compare conversion rate on creative with a clear buyer signal versus generic creative in the same broad ad set.

title: Exclude existing customers from every cold campaign, sized to the repurchase cycle
hypothesis: If existing customers are excluded from every cold campaign with a window set to the repurchase cycle, then cold concepts get judged fairly because repeat buyers stop making a weak concept look strong.

signal.check: Cold Meta or TikTok campaigns have no customer exclusion, or the exclusion window does not match the store's repurchase cycle.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one example showed about half of top-of-funnel budget going to existing customers

risk.note: Depends on a working customer file sync; a broken sync silently lets existing customers back into cold.

prerequisites: Synced customer file (Klaviyo to Meta, CSV to TikTok)
Repurchase cycle length
steps: Confirm the customer file is synced and current.
Set the exclusion window to 2 years as a default starting point.
Shorten the window to the brand's own repurchase cycle for short-cycle categories.
Apply the exclusion to every cold campaign on every platform, including TikTok retargeting exclusions.

test.method: Check audience segment breakdown after applying exclusions; existing customer share in cold should be near 0%.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after applying exclusions.

title: Never launch placement, age or gender campaigns from breakdown ROAS
hypothesis: If placement, age and gender breakdowns are never used to launch new campaigns, then spend stops chasing a blended number because breakdown data ignores incremental return.

signal.check: A breakdown, such as Stories showing 4x versus Feed at 3x, is being used to justify a new placement, age or gender campaign.

risk.note: Refusing a proposed campaign; no account change.

steps: Pull the breakdown that is prompting the new campaign idea.
Remember breakdown data is blended and ignores incremental return.
Do not launch a placement, age or gender campaign from it.
If curious, run a proper incrementality or lift test instead.

test.method: Track how many placement or demographic campaigns get proposed versus rejected under this rule.

title: Remove Audience Network app rewards placement from store or engaged-view campaigns
hypothesis: If the Audience Network app rewards placement is removed from store and engaged-view campaigns, then wasted spend drops because that placement has not been seen to drive a purchase.

signal.check: A store-traffic or engaged-view campaign includes Audience Network app rewards placement.

risk.note: A placement removal, not a targeting or budget change.

prerequisites: Access to placement settings
steps: Open the placement breakdown for store or engaged-view campaigns.
Check for Audience Network app rewards placement.
Remove it from the placement list.
Recheck placement breakdown after the next read window.

test.method: Compare CPA before and after removing the placement.

title: Default to CBO for efficiency, but switch to ABO at high AOV with low daily order volume
hypothesis: If CBO is the default and ABO is used instead at high AOV with low daily order volume, then spend efficiency improves because CBO cannot lean on CTR and CPC signals when there are too few daily conversions to learn from.

signal.check: The account uses CBO while running at very high AOV with only a handful of orders a day, so CBO likely falls back to soft signals instead of conversion signals.

expected_effect.size: unknown; CBO example shows about 10% lower ROI under ABO at the small tier as the cost of forced testing

risk.note: Switching budget type can shift delivery; monitor the first read window closely.

prerequisites: AOV and average daily order count
steps: Check AOV and average orders per day for the account.
If AOV is very high and daily orders are low, switch from CBO to ABO for that campaign.
For other accounts, choose CBO for efficiency or ABO for controlled risk based on owner preference.
Record which budget type was chosen and why.

test.method: Compare ROAS and spend distribution across ad sets before and after switching budget type.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the switch.

title: At large spend, run CBO with ad-set minimum and maximum spend limits instead of pure CBO
hypothesis: If a large-spend CBO campaign sets ad-set minimum and maximum spend limits at roughly a 60% directed, 40% free split, then risk concentration drops because no single ad set can take all the budget or none of it.

signal.check: A CBO campaign at large spend has no ad-set spend limits and one or two ad sets are taking almost all the budget.

risk.note: Overkill and extra oversight work below about $10,000 a month; reserve for large accounts.

prerequisites: A CBO campaign with uneven spend distribution
steps: Check spend distribution across ad sets in the CBO campaign.
Set a minimum spend limit so no live ad set gets starved.
Set a maximum spend limit so no single ad set can take the whole budget, for example a 40% cap.
Review the split monthly and adjust the limits.

test.method: Compare spend concentration and ROAS before and after setting spend limits.

title: Test a seasonal rotation: CBO in Q4 peak, ABO in Q1 for clean testing
hypothesis: If the account runs CBO through Q4 peak and switches to ABO in Q1, then test reads stay clean because Q4's inflated conversion rate stops disguising weak concepts.

signal.check: The account uses the same budget type year round despite a strong Q4 seasonal swing in conversion rate.

risk.note: A scheduled switch, not a permanent structural change.

prerequisites: A seasonal sales calendar
steps: Plan to switch the account to CBO ahead of the Q4 peak.
Switch back to ABO in Q1 once the peak season ends.
Read Q1 test results knowing Q4's conversion rate no longer applies.
Repeat the rotation each year and compare year over year.

test.method: Compare Q1 test kill and keep accuracy under this rotation versus a year without it.
test.read_point: Across one full Q4 to Q1 cycle.

title: Ignore cost and bid caps under about $200k a month; pick a bid strategy by business constraint
hypothesis: If cost caps and bid caps are ignored below about $200,000 a month and the bid strategy is chosen by business constraint instead, then time spent fiddling with bids goes to creative instead, where it pays more.

signal.check: The team spends time daily adjusting cost caps or bid caps on an account well under $200,000 a month in spend.

expected_effect.size: unknown; daily bid tweaks might squeeze about 5% for an hour of work a day

risk.note: A time-allocation decision, not an account risk.

steps: Check the account's monthly spend against the about $200,000 threshold.
Below it, use lowest cost bidding by default unless a CPA ceiling or bid ceiling is a real constraint.
Above about $250,000 a month, diversify bid strategy across campaigns.
Redirect time saved from daily bid tweaking into creative production.

test.method: Track hours spent on bid adjustments before and after adopting this rule, and compare CPA.

title: Set cost caps and bidding at ad set level, never at ad level
hypothesis: If cost caps and bid strategy are only ever set at ad set level, then ad-level ROAS stops misleading anyone because ads correctly inherit optimisation from their ad set.

signal.check: Anyone is looking for a bid or cost cap setting at the individual ad level instead of the ad set.

risk.note: A settings-location fix, not a targeting or budget change.

steps: Confirm all bid and cost cap settings live at ad set level.
Remove any confusion about ad-level bidding from team documentation.
Remind the team that ad-level ROAS is unreliable partly because of this inheritance.
Use ad set level settings consistently across the account.

test.method: Check settings placement during the next structure audit.

title: Size every creative test with a kill-rule threshold: spend to 3x to 5x target CPA before judging
hypothesis: If every concept ad set spends 3x to 5x its target CPA before being judged, then kill calls stop happening on noise because the ad set has had a fair shot to convert.

signal.check: A test is being judged or killed before it has spent at least 3 times the target CPA at the concept ad set level.

risk.note: A sizing rule to apply before launch, not a change once a test is live.

prerequisites: A target CPA or ROAS derived from margin
steps: Set the target CPA for the concept before launch.
Set the kill-rule threshold at 3x target CPA, or 5x for a stricter yes or no read.
Do not judge the ad set until it reaches that spend threshold.
Write the decision table (keep, yellow, kill) before launch.

test.method: Track how many tests get killed before reaching the threshold versus after adopting this rule.

title: Size test budgets with the formula: target conversions times CPA divided by test days
hypothesis: If daily test budget is set as target conversions times expected CPA divided by test days, then the test gets a fair number of conversions in its read window instead of an arbitrary daily spend.

signal.check: A test's daily budget was picked without calculating target conversions times expected CPA divided by planned test days.

expected_effect.size: unknown; example 20 conversions x $100 CPA / 14 days is about $143 a day

risk.note: A sizing formula, not a spend increase by itself.

prerequisites: A target CPA and a chosen conversion count for the read
steps: Pick the number of conversions needed for a confident read, such as 5 for a first screen or 10 to 20 for a scale decision.
Multiply by the expected CPA.
Divide by the number of test days.
Set that as the daily budget and confirm it is also at least 3x target CPA over the window.

test.method: Compare read confidence and kill accuracy for tests sized with the formula versus guessed budgets.

title: Never derive test budgets from Meta's 50-conversions-in-7-days learning rule
hypothesis: If test budgets are set from target CPA and read window instead of Meta's 50-conversions-in-7-days rule, then most accounts avoid an unrealistic daily budget because that rule implies about $714 a day at a $100 CPA.

signal.check: A proposed test budget is being justified by hitting 50 conversions in 7 days rather than by target CPA and read window.

risk.note: Refusing an oversized budget request; no account risk.

steps: Check whether a proposed budget was derived from the 50-in-7 learning rule.
If so, recalculate it using the kill-rule or formula method instead.
Explain to stakeholders why exiting learning is not the goal.
Log the smaller, realistic budget instead.

test.method: Track proposed versus approved test budgets over a quarter.

title: Match test read windows to purchase cycle and volume; never read under 5 days below $50k a month
hypothesis: If the read window is matched to purchase cycle and conversion volume, with a floor of 5 days below $50,000 a month spend, then decisions stop reacting to daily noise because the window has enough conversions to be stable.

signal.check: A test is being read or acted on after 1 to 2 days, or on a spend level too small to support a confident read.

risk.note: A read-timing discipline, not a spend change.

prerequisites: Revenue by weekday and time from first visit to purchase, if available
steps: Default the read window to 1 week.
Shorten to 3 to 4 days only for large, stable brands with short purchase cycles.
Extend to 10 to 14 days for tiny budgets, long purchase cycles, or strong weekday swings.
Never read or act under 5 days when monthly spend is below $50,000, and never act on 1 day of data.

test.method: Compare decision reversals (killed too early, then would have won) before and after fixing the read window.
test.read_point: At each test's fixed read date.

title: Never judge or kill an ad on $1 to $2 of spend
hypothesis: If no ad or ad set is judged before a minimum meaningful spend, then good concepts stop being cut early because a few dollars of spend cannot show a fair result.

signal.check: An ad or ad set is being killed or praised after only $1 to $2 of spend or a few impressions.

risk.note: A patience rule, not a targeting or budget change.

steps: Set a minimum spend or impression floor before any ad gets a verdict.
Hold off on kill or scale decisions until that floor is reached.
Do not chase Meta's learning-phase exit as a proxy for readiness.
Apply the same floor consistently across the account.

test.method: Track how many early-kill reversals happen after this rule is adopted.

title: Test ads that differ by benefit, price point or persona, not just crop or color
hypothesis: If test batches vary by product benefit, price point or persona instead of crop or color, then new audiences actually get reached because near-identical ads collapse into one delivery group and reach nobody new.

signal.check: A test batch is made of ads that share the same benefit, price and persona and differ only in crop, color or minor edit.

expected_effect.size: unknown; near-identical ads can read as far fewer unique ads to the delivery system

risk.note: A creative briefing change, not an account structure change.

prerequisites: A concept matrix covering multiple benefits, price points or personas
steps: Review the current test batch for real concept diversity, not just visual variation.
Brief new ads that change the benefit claim, the price framing, or the target persona.
Keep visual-only variations as hook variations inside an existing concept, not as new concepts.
Count diversity by concept, not by number of files.

test.method: Compare cold reach and CPA for concept-diverse batches versus crop-only variation batches.

title: Never run creative tests inside the scaling campaign
hypothesis: If new creative tests never launch inside the scaling campaign, then the scaling campaign keeps its efficiency because it is never disrupted by unproven ads.

signal.check: New or untested ads are being added directly into the scaling campaign instead of the testing campaign.

risk.note: A process rule; enforce it in the launch checklist.

prerequisites: A separate testing campaign and a scaling campaign
steps: Confirm the account has a separate testing campaign and scaling campaign.
Route all new creative into the testing campaign only.
Move an ad into the scaling campaign only after it is a confirmed equilibrium winner.
Check the scaling campaign monthly for any untested ads that crept in.

test.method: Audit the scaling campaign monthly for any newly added untested ads.

title: Launch about 1 new ad per $1,000 of monthly spend, with diminishing returns at very large spend
hypothesis: If new ad output tracks about 1 ad per $1,000 of monthly spend, then creative stops being the bottleneck because volume matches the account's real capacity to test.

signal.check: New ads launched per month is well below monthly spend divided by $1,000, especially in the $50k to $250k range where 100 to 300 ads a month is the benchmark.

expected_effect.size: about 1 ad per $1,000 of monthly spend; 100 to 300 at $50k to $250k; diminishing above $1M

risk.note: A production-planning target; at very large spend replace it with a winner-churn model instead.

prerequisites: Monthly ad spend
Creative production capacity
steps: Calculate monthly spend divided by $1,000 as the target new-ad count.
Compare against actual new ads launched last month.
If far below target, flag creative volume as the bottleneck and brief more.
At very large spend, replace this heuristic with a winner-churn or average-winner model if that data exists.

test.method: Track new ads launched per month against the target for 3 consecutive months.

title: Hit the concept-count band for your spend tier
hypothesis: If the number of live and testing concepts matches the spend-tier band, then fatigue risk drops because no single concept is forced to carry spend it was never built for.

signal.check: The account runs at $200,000 a month or more spend with only 1 concept, or otherwise sits well outside its spend-tier concept-count band.

expected_effect.size: under $100k: 1 to 3 concepts; $100k to $500k: about 2 winning, 2 to 6 testing; above $500k: 3+ winning, 4 to 5 core funnels

risk.note: A creative planning target, not an account structure change.

prerequisites: Monthly spend
List of live concepts
steps: Count current winning and testing concepts.
Compare against the band for the account's spend tier.
If below band, brief new concepts, not more variations of existing ones.
Recheck the count monthly as spend changes.

test.method: Track concept count against the band and frequency trend on the top concept over 2 months.

title: Judge and move budget at the ad-set level, never on a single ad's ROAS
hypothesis: If keep, kill and budget calls are made at the ad-set level instead of the single-ad level, then good ads stop getting cut because ad-level ROAS is unreliable under multi-ad sequencing and view-through credit.

signal.check: An ad is about to be paused or its budget cut based on that single ad's own ROAS, while the ad set it lives in is at KPI.

risk.note: A discipline change in how decisions get made, not a targeting change.

steps: Before pausing or scaling any single ad, check the ad set's overall CPA or ROAS against target.
If the ad set is at KPI, do not pause the ad based on its own number alone.
Ask one question: is this ad set, with this set of ads, at KPI.
Reserve ad-level reads for creative briefs, not budget moves.

test.method: Track how many single-ad pause decisions get reversed after adopting ad-set-level judging.
test.read_point: Ongoing, reviewed at each weekly read.

title: Inside a winning ad set, use spend share only to brief new creative, never to move budget
hypothesis: If spend share inside an at-KPI ad set is used only to tell the creative team which ads to make more of, then creative output improves because the signal that already exists in the account gets used without being misapplied to budget.

signal.check: An ad set is at KPI and some ads inside it are clearly taking most of the spend, but nobody has turned that into a creative brief.

expected_effect.size: unknown; of 20 ads in an ad set, maybe 4 take spend

risk.note: Only valid inside an ad set already confirmed at KPI; never use it for budget moves.

prerequisites: An ad set confirmed at KPI
steps: Sort ads inside the at-KPI ad set by spend.
List the top 2 to 4 ads by spend as the make-more-like-this brief.
Send the brief to the creative team.
Do not use this ranking to raise or cut any single ad's budget.

test.method: Track how many creative briefs come from spend-share reads versus other sources over a quarter.

title: Apply the keep, yellow, kill decision table at 3x to 5x target CPA
hypothesis: If concept ad sets are read against a fixed table (3 to 4 conversions at 3x CPA keeps, 2 is yellow, 0 to 1 kills; 5x CPA is a straight yes or no), then kill calls stop being subjective because every ad set is judged by the same numbers.

signal.check: An ad set has reached its spend threshold and nobody has applied a fixed keep, yellow, kill table to decide its fate.

risk.note: Applies to concept ad sets, not single ads.

prerequisites: A test sized with the kill-rule method (3x to 5x target CPA)
steps: At 3x target CPA: keep at 3 to 4 conversions, mark yellow at 2 and extend about 1 more CPA of spend, kill at 0 to 1.
At 5x target CPA: treat the result as a straight yes or no.
Write the specific numbers that triggered each call in the decision log.
Apply the same table to every concept ad set for consistency.

test.method: Track how many kill or keep calls match the table's numbers versus gut calls, and compare CPA outcomes.

title: Raise winning ad set budgets in steps sized to the read window, not a fixed percentage
hypothesis: If budget raises on winning ad sets are sized to the read window rather than a fixed percentage, then scale-ups stop getting judged on noise because the raise is always read after enough days to see past the lag.

signal.check: A winning ad set's budget was raised and then judged on same-day or next-day revenue instead of over a full read window.

expected_effect.size: unknown; about 20% a day is a common default at the small tier, larger steps are used when the lag is accepted

risk.note: A large raise with a short read window can look like a loss during the lag; always wait for the full window.

prerequisites: An ad set confirmed at KPI over one full read window
steps: Default to about a 20% daily raise for accounts under about $50,000 a month.
Allow larger steps above that if the owner accepts a 7-day lag before judging the raise.
Log the date and size of every raise.
Never judge a raise on same-day revenue; wait for the full read window.

test.method: Compare ROAS 7 days after each raise against the pre-raise baseline.
test.read_point: 7 days or more after each raise.

title: Confirm a winner acquires new customers under 7-day click before briefing more of it
hypothesis: If any top-spending ad is checked for its new-customer ROAS under 7-day click before more of it gets briefed, then creative budget stops chasing a false winner because blended ROAS can hide a much weaker true acquisition number.

signal.check: A top-spending ad is being scaled or briefed for more variants based on its blended ROAS, without checking its new-customer segment ROAS under 7-day click.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one example showed 12.84x blended, about 5x new-segment, 1.71x new-segment under incremental attribution

risk.note: Briefing more of a false winner spends real creative budget against bad data.

prerequisites: Audience segment breakdown available (new, engaged, existing)
steps: Open the ad at ad level and note its blended ROAS and frequency.
Pull the audience segment breakdown and read the new-segment ROAS.
Add the incremental attribution comparison column and read the new-segment number there too.
Only brief more of the ad once its new-customer 7-day-click ROAS clears the target.

test.method: Compare blended, new-segment and incremental ROAS for every ad before approving a new creative brief from it.

title: Do not ride one winner; clone it into variants and keep a creative pipeline running
hypothesis: If a dominant winner is cloned into variants while other concepts keep running, then the account survives the winner's eventual fatigue because a backup pipeline is already in place.

signal.check: One ad or concept carries most of the account's spend and every other concept has been turned off.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources call turning everything else off amateur hour

risk.note: Fatigue is a when, not an if, for a dominant winner with no backup.

prerequisites: A confirmed dominant winner
steps: Identify the ad or concept taking the largest share of spend.
Brief variant hooks and angles of that concept to extend its life.
Keep at least 1 to 2 other concepts alive at meaningful spend as a backup.
Set a spend-share cap, such as 40%, or consciously choose to double down instead.

test.method: Track spend concentration and frequency on the top concept monthly.

title: Rescue high-conviction, CBO-starved ads in a small separate ad set, capped and logged
hypothesis: If ads the CBO starved of spend are re-launched in a small, capped separate ad set only when the team has high conviction, then good creative the algorithm missed gets a second chance without risking the main budget.

signal.check: Ads with 0 or near-0 spend after a full read window are being ignored entirely, with no rescue process.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source claims about 20% of rescued ads become winners

risk.note: This is one presenter's tactic and conflicts with trusting the algorithm's allocation; use only with a hard budget cap and a log.

prerequisites: A CBO campaign that has run a full read window
steps: List ads with 0 or near-0 spend after the window.
Keep only the ones with a written reason for high conviction.
Launch them in a separate ad set with a small budget sized from the kill-rule method.
Read after the standard window and log the hit rate; move winners into the normal concept structure.

test.method: Track the hit rate of rescued ads against the account's normal new-concept hit rate.
test.read_point: At the standard read window after launch.

title: Check that every ad set's planned budget can actually reach its read-spend threshold in the test window
hypothesis: If daily budget times test days is checked against the read-spend threshold for every ad set before launch, then unreadable tests stop happening because a plan that cannot reach its own threshold gets fixed before it wastes the window.

signal.check: A test plan sets a read point, such as 3x target CPA, and a daily budget per ad set, without checking whether daily budget times days actually reaches that spend.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one run found 4 of 12 ad sets in a single plan could not reach their read spend

risk.note: A planning check before launch; catching this early avoids wasting the whole test window.

prerequisites: A test plan with daily budgets and a stated read point per ad set
steps: Build a table: ad set, daily budget, planned days, total spend, required read spend.
Mark each ad set readable or not readable based on whether total spend reaches the read spend.
For any not readable, merge ad sets, cut variant count, lengthen the window, or mark it not readable in advance.
Confirm every control ad set has spend in the last 7 days before using it as a benchmark.

test.method: Check the readable-or-not table again at the actual read date to confirm the plan held.
test.read_point: Before launch, and again at the read date.

title: Find each winner's spend equilibrium by stepping budget up until ROAS turns unprofitable, then pull back
hypothesis: If a winning ad set's budget is raised in steps until ROAS turns unprofitable and then pulled back, then its true spend capacity gets recorded because the level where results hold becomes a known number instead of a guess.

signal.check: A winning ad set is running well above target ROAS with strong soft metrics, but no one has found or recorded its spend equilibrium.

expected_effect.size: unknown; example equilibrium found around $300 a day

risk.note: Repeated raises and pullbacks can cause short-term ROAS swings; read each step over a full window.

prerequisites: A winning ad set well above target ROAS for one full read window
steps: Raise the ad set's daily budget in steps.
Hold each step for a full read window before judging it.
When ROAS turns unprofitable, pull back to the last good level.
Record that level as the creative's spend capacity.

test.method: Track ROAS at each budget step until the equilibrium point is found and confirmed stable.
test.read_point: After each budget step's full read window.

title: Move only confirmed equilibrium winners into a dedicated scaling campaign
hypothesis: If only ad sets that have found their spend equilibrium move into a dedicated scaling campaign, excluding existing customers and running no tests inside it, then scale spend holds up because only proven creative sits there.

signal.check: An ad set is being moved into a scaling campaign without having found its spend equilibrium, or the scaling campaign includes tests or lacks exclusions.

expected_effect.size: unknown; worth it from about $400 a day per asset, not worth it at about $60 a day

risk.note: Moving a winner risks a short delivery reset; keep the original ad set running in parallel.

prerequisites: A confirmed equilibrium winner at or above about $400 a day capacity
steps: Confirm the ad set's equilibrium spend is about $400 a day or more.
Build or use a CBO scaling campaign with one ad set holding the same post IDs.
Exclude existing customers and run no creative tests inside it.
Keep the original ad set running; refresh top post IDs every 1 to 2 weeks at large spend.

test.method: Track scaling campaign ROAS at campaign level and compare to the original ad set's equilibrium ROAS.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the move.

title: Judge every budget raise over 7 or more days, never on same-day revenue
hypothesis: If a budget raise is always judged over 7 or more days instead of same-day revenue, then good raises stop getting reversed early because new audiences need several exposures before they buy.

signal.check: A recent budget raise is being judged as a failure based on the first day or two of revenue after the raise.

expected_effect.size: unknown; raises above 20% are fine as long as the dip is read as a lag, not a learning reset

risk.note: A read-timing rule, not a change to the raise itself.

prerequisites: A recent budget raise with a logged date
steps: Log the date of every budget raise.
Wait at least 7 days before judging the raise's ROAS.
Do not treat a same-day or next-day dip as a learning reset.
If ROAS is still weak after 7 days, then reconsider the raise.

test.method: Compare same-day judgment outcomes versus 7-day judgment outcomes for the same set of raises.

title: Agree a scale ceiling with the owner: GP-to-CAC band by default, near-break-even only as a deliberate choice
hypothesis: If the owner explicitly picks a scale ceiling, either a GP-to-CAC band or a near-break-even cash-backed target, then scaling stops drifting past what the business can safely fund because the ceiling was agreed in advance.

signal.check: The account is scaling spend with no agreed scale ceiling between platform ROAS, GP-to-CAC and cash position.

risk.note: Scaling to near break-even without a cash and loss limit risks running the business out of cash.

prerequisites: GP-to-CAC and retention data
The owner's risk appetite
steps: Present the GP-to-CAC band option (2 to 3 to scale, below 1 a warning) to the owner.
Present the near-break-even, net-cash-in-30-days option as an alternative.
Have the owner pick one in writing, with a cash and loss limit if choosing near break-even.
Use the chosen ceiling consistently in every scale decision.

test.method: Track actual scale decisions against the agreed ceiling for 3 months.

title: When doubling down on a winner, shift creative volume toward it and build the funnel around it
hypothesis: If creative volume shifts toward a confirmed winner and the funnel (custom landing page, named bundle, testimonials) is built around it, then the winning concept converts even better because the whole path now matches the ad's promise.

signal.check: A concept is confirmed as a real new-customer winner but still runs on a generic landing page with no dedicated bundle or testimonials.

expected_effect.size: unknown; example shift is 120 ads for the winner versus 40 for the rest, from an even 50-50 split

risk.note: Requires the winner to already be confirmed on new customers; check LTV of the concept first.

prerequisites: A winner confirmed on new-customer 7-day-click ROAS
LTV by acquiring concept, if available
steps: Confirm the concept is a real new-customer winner and check its LTV if available.
Shift creative production ratio toward the winning concept, for example 120 ads to 40 for everything else.
Build a custom landing page, a named bundle, and testimonials specific to the concept.
Track conversion rate and AOV on the new funnel versus the generic one.

test.method: Compare conversion rate and AOV before and after building the dedicated funnel.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the funnel launches.

title: Judge a SKU-level scale-up on store-side new-customer sales for that SKU, not platform ROAS
hypothesis: If a scale-up that concentrates on one SKU is judged by new-customer sales of that SKU in store data, then a false scale win gets caught because platform ROAS alone can overstate the result.

signal.check: A budget increase concentrated on one SKU is being judged only by platform ROAS, with no check of that SKU's new-customer sales in store data.

risk.note: Store-wide reads need a longer test or bigger budget change; confirm the SKU was not promoted elsewhere in the window.

prerequisites: SKU-level sales split new vs returning, daily
steps: Pull daily SKU-level sales split new versus returning for the scaled SKU.
Compare new-customer SKU sales before and after the budget change.
Confirm the SKU was not also promoted elsewhere, such as email or another channel, during the window.
If new-customer SKU sales did not rise despite platform ROAS looking good, treat platform ROAS as overstated and revert.

test.method: Compare new-customer SKU sales for at least 2 weeks before and after the scale-up.
test.read_point: 2 or more weeks after the budget change.

title: Check live stock before raising budget or moving an ad set into the scaling campaign
hypothesis: If live stock is checked before any budget raise or scaling move, then wasted spend drops because no concept gets more budget for a SKU that is about to run out.

signal.check: A budget raise or move into the scaling campaign is being proposed without checking the current stock level of the SKU being scaled.

risk.note: No library source gives a live-stock check before scaling; verify against the brand's own inventory data.

prerequisites: Current stock level by SKU
steps: Check current stock and days of stock remaining for the SKU being scaled.
If stock is low or the SKU is close to out of stock, hold the budget raise.
If stock supports it, proceed with the raise or scaling move.
Repeat this check before every future raise on that SKU.

test.method: Track stockout incidents that followed a budget raise before and after adopting this check.

title: Set every cold Meta campaign to 7-day click attribution for reads and optimisation
hypothesis: If every cold campaign is set to 7-day click for optimisation and reads, then decisions track the actual path from ad to checkout because view-through credit stops pulling spend to ads that only win on views.

signal.check: Any cold campaign is optimising or being read on 7-day click plus 1-day view, or on a mix of attribution settings.

expected_effect.size: unknown; view-through pulls spend to view-winning ads and over-credits existing customers

risk.note: Changing attribution settings can shift which ads win spend; re-read rankings after 1 full window before killing anything.

prerequisites: Access to campaign attribution settings
steps: Check the attribution setting on every cold campaign.
Set 7-day click as the setting for optimisation and reads.
Turn off 1-day view for budget decisions.
Re-read ad and ad-set rankings after one full window before making kill calls on the new numbers.

test.method: Compare ad-set rankings before and after switching to 7-day click for one full read window.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the switch.

title: Use the same attribution setting on every campaign in the account
hypothesis: If every campaign uses the same attribution setting, then ROAS becomes comparable across campaigns because mixed settings stop quietly changing what a number means from one campaign to the next.

signal.check: Different campaigns in the same account use different attribution settings, so ROAS numbers cannot be compared directly.

risk.note: A settings audit, not a targeting change.

steps: List the attribution setting on every campaign.
Flag any campaign that differs from the account standard.
Set every campaign to the same attribution window, matching the 7-day click rule.
Recheck at every structure audit.

test.method: Audit attribution consistency across campaigns each month.

title: Use incremental attribution as a comparison column only, never as the optimisation target
hypothesis: If incremental attribution is read only as a comparison column and never set as the optimisation target, then decisions stay grounded because it is a modelled factor from other advertisers' lift studies, not this account's measured result.

signal.check: A campaign is optimising toward incremental attribution, or incremental attribution is being treated as the measure of success rather than a check.

expected_effect.size: unknown; example factor of 0.2x on a retargeting segment turned a 10x number into 2x

risk.note: Misreading a modelled factor as a measured lift can hide real weakness in retargeting or DPA.

prerequisites: Access to the compare-attribution-settings column
steps: Add the incremental attribution comparison column to campaign reports.
Read it beside 7-day click and blended ROAS, never in place of them.
Never set a campaign's optimisation goal to incremental attribution.
Use it mainly to sanity-check DPA and retargeting numbers.

test.method: Track the gap between incremental attribution and 7-day click for retargeting and DPA monthly.

title: Run a Conversion Lift or geo-lift test when platform ROAS and aMER still disagree after tightening attribution
hypothesis: If a Conversion Lift or geo-lift test runs whenever platform ROAS and aMER still disagree after attribution is tightened, then the real answer replaces a guess because a controlled holdout measures incremental impact directly.

signal.check: Platform ROAS and acquisition MER still disagree meaningfully after 7-day click and comparison columns have been checked.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the test itself runs about 25 days

risk.note: Design detail for the lift test itself lives outside this domain; this idea only covers when to trigger one.

prerequisites: Enough spend and scale to support a lift or geo test
A defined test design (Conversion Lift or geo-lift)
steps: Confirm platform ROAS and aMER still disagree after tightening attribution settings.
Set up a Conversion Lift Test (user-level holdout) or a causal geo-lift test.
Set test parameters in advance and run for about 25 days.
Use the lift result to decide whether to switch attribution settings or accept the platform number.

test.method: Compare the lift-measured incremental result to the platform-reported ROAS for the same period.
test.read_point: At the end of the lift test, about 25 days.

title: Build a monthly new-customer view: CAC, first-purchase gross profit and GP-to-CAC
hypothesis: If CAC, first-purchase gross profit and GP-to-CAC are tracked monthly using real margin, then acquisition health becomes visible because repeat revenue can no longer hide a weak first-order economics story.

signal.check: The account has no monthly view of CAC, first-purchase gross profit or GP-to-CAC, or the view uses a flat gross-margin assumption instead of real numbers.

risk.note: Never use a flat gross-margin assumption; pull real monthly margin.

prerequisites: Orders with a new vs returning flag
Monthly gross margin
steps: Pull new customers per month for 2 to 2.5 years back.
Calculate CAC as spend divided by new customers.
Calculate first-purchase gross profit from real AOV and margin, not a flat assumption.
Calculate GP-to-CAC and track the trend monthly.

test.method: Track whether CAC rising is paired with rising volume (fine) or flat volume (a bottleneck).

title: Score first-purchase GP-to-CAC against fixed bands before deciding to hold, scale or spend more
hypothesis: If first-purchase GP-to-CAC is scored against fixed bands every month, then the scale decision stops being a guess because the number tells you to hold, scale, or spend more.

signal.check: GP-to-CAC is calculated but not compared against a fixed band to decide whether to hold, scale, or spend more.

expected_effect.size: below 1 losing money; 1 to 2 hold; 2 to 3 scale; above 3 spend more

risk.note: Strong retention can justify a lower band; weak retention needs a higher one. Assumes no acquisition channel is left out of CAC.

prerequisites: Monthly GP-to-CAC from the new-customer P&L view
steps: Calculate first-purchase GP-to-CAC for the month.
Compare against the band: below 1 losing, 1 to 2 hold, 2 to 3 scale, above 3 spend more.
Adjust the band up for weak retention or down for strong retention.
Use the resulting call as an input to the scale ceiling decision.

test.method: Track GP-to-CAC against the band monthly and note every band crossing.

title: Do not tighten Google attribution windows or copy Meta attribution rules onto Google
hypothesis: If Google's attribution stays untouched by Meta's rules, then Google reporting stays accurate because Google's attribution model is not the same problem as Meta's view-through inflation.

signal.check: Someone is proposing to tighten Google's attribution window or apply the same 7-day-click logic used on Meta.

risk.note: Google structure and attribution belong to a different domain; check there before making changes.

steps: Confirm any attribution change request is specifically about Meta, not Google.
Leave Google's attribution settings as they are.
Address Google-specific issues, like brand versus non-brand separation, in the Google Ads domain instead.
Document this boundary for the team.

test.method: Audit whether Google settings changed in the last quarter and why.

title: On TikTok, read 7-day click and reconcile TikTok-reported purchases with store orders
hypothesis: If TikTok is read on 7-day click and its reported purchases are reconciled with store orders, then TikTok's real return becomes visible because 1-day view inflates ROAS a lot on this platform.

signal.check: TikTok campaigns are being judged on default attribution with no reconciliation against store order counts.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source expects TikTok to drop to about aMER or lower once read at 7-day click

risk.note: A reporting and reconciliation habit, not a campaign change.

prerequisites: Store orders for the TikTok-attributed period
steps: Set TikTok's attribution comparison to 7-day click.
Pull TikTok-reported purchases for the period.
Compare against actual store orders for the same window.
Use the reconciled number, not the raw platform number, for CPA decisions.

test.method: Track the gap between TikTok-reported purchases and store orders monthly.

title: For marketplace-heavy stores, reconcile marketplace sales separately from platform ROAS and aMER
hypothesis: If platform ROAS and aMER get a separate reconciliation for marketplace-driven sales, then acquisition numbers stop being wrong because a meaningful share of ad-driven sales happens outside the pixel's reach.

signal.check: A meaningful share of paid social's sales happen on Amazon, Flipkart or another marketplace outside the brand's own checkout, but ROAS and aMER are calculated as if all sales are on-site.

risk.note: No library source for marketplace-outside-pixel attribution; verify against the brand's own marketplace sales data.

prerequisites: Marketplace sales data with a way to attribute some share to paid social
steps: Estimate the share of marketplace sales likely driven by paid social, using promo timing or marketplace ad spend as a proxy.
Add that estimate to the aMER calculation as a separate, clearly marked line.
Do not let platform ROAS alone represent total impact when marketplace sales are meaningful.
Revisit the estimate whenever marketplace mix changes.

test.method: Compare aMER with and without the marketplace adjustment and check which better matches known business growth.

title: In cash-on-delivery markets, reconcile store orders net of COD returns before trusting platform ROAS
hypothesis: If store orders are reconciled net of cash-on-delivery returns before trusting platform ROAS, then reported performance stops overstating results because COD orders that bounce back never counted as real revenue.

signal.check: A meaningful share of orders are cash-on-delivery and platform ROAS is being trusted without netting out COD return and non-collection rates.

risk.note: No library source for COD reconciliation; verify against the brand's own COD return data.

prerequisites: COD order and return data from the store
steps: Pull the COD return or non-collection rate for the period.
Net confirmed, paid orders out of the total platform-reported purchase count.
Recalculate ROAS and CAC on the netted order count.
Track the COD return rate over time to catch delivery or courier problems early.

test.method: Compare platform-reported ROAS against COD-netted ROAS for the same period.

title: Win impressions with a sharper hook and clearer offer instead of raising the bid
hypothesis: If the hook and offer are sharpened to raise expected click and purchase rate instead of raising the bid, then the account buys cheaper reach because a stronger action rate can beat a higher bid in the auction.

signal.check: CPMs or CPAs are rising and the response has been to raise bids rather than test a sharper hook or clearer price on the ad itself.

expected_effect.size: unknown; example a $0.50 bid can beat $1 with a better action rate

risk.note: Action rate and quality are rear-view diagnostics that cannot be set directly; diversify creative rather than chase the number.

prerequisites: A running ad with room to test a sharper hook or clearer price
steps: Identify an ad set where CPM or CPA has been rising.
Brief a variant with a sharper hook or clearer price framing instead of raising the bid.
Launch it beside the original at the same bid.
Compare delivered cost per result between the two.

test.method: Compare CPM and CPA between the sharper-hook variant and the original at the same bid.

title: Diversify creative before a narrow-persona callout saturates its cluster and drifts to colder audiences
hypothesis: If new creative concepts are briefed before a narrow, specific callout ad saturates its buying cluster, then ROAS tapering gets avoided because the delivery system is not forced to drift into unconvinced, colder people to keep spending.

signal.check: A narrow, specific-callout ad has been running at meaningful spend, such as around $10,000, with no new concept briefed yet to follow it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; illustration is saturation after around $10,000 on a very specific callout ad

risk.note: A creative-pipeline timing decision, not a targeting change.

prerequisites: A narrow-persona callout ad approaching meaningful cumulative spend
steps: Track cumulative spend on narrow, specific-callout ads.
Brief a new concept before the ad nears its likely saturation point.
Watch for rising frequency and tapering ROAS as the early warning sign.
Launch the new concept in its own ad set rather than editing the saturating one.

test.method: Compare ROAS trend on accounts that pre-brief new concepts versus those that wait for tapering to start.

title: Pass every order and its value cleanly from checkout to the pixel and CAPI
hypothesis: If every order and its value passes cleanly from checkout to the pixel and CAPI, then bidding stops being blind because a store missing real orders under-estimates its own best customers and loses auctions it should win.

signal.check: Meta or TikTok purchase counts are noticeably lower than actual backend orders, meaning tracking is dropping a meaningful share of conversions.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a store missing 30% of real orders is bidding blind on its best customers

risk.note: Treat this as required plumbing owned by the measurement domain; do not expect a performance gain from raising EMQ alone.

prerequisites: Backend order count for comparison
Pixel and CAPI already installed
steps: Compare Meta or TikTok reported purchases against backend order count for the same period.
Identify where orders are being lost: missing events, blocked pixel, broken CAPI.
Fix the gap with the measurement team or domain.
Recheck the match rate monthly.

test.method: Track the gap between platform-reported purchases and backend orders monthly.

title: Read 30-day frequency by audience segment, not as a blended percentage
hypothesis: If frequency is read by audience segment on a 30-day window instead of as one blended number, then fatigue gets caught early because existing, engaged and new segments each have their own healthy range.

signal.check: Frequency is reported as one blended account-wide number instead of broken out by new, engaged and existing segments over 30 days.

expected_effect.size: unknown; existing customers should stay below 7 per 30 days, engaged around 14 signals too much middle-funnel creative

risk.note: A reporting change, not a targeting change by itself.

prerequisites: Audience segments defined (new, engaged, existing)
steps: Confirm audience segments are defined in advertiser settings.
Pull 30-day frequency separately for new, engaged and existing segments.
Compare each against its own healthy range instead of one blended target.
Flag any segment outside range for follow-up.

test.method: Track segment frequency monthly and flag any segment trending toward its ceiling.

title: When frequency rises with flat cold reach, fix the creative mix by awareness stage before touching exclusions
hypothesis: If a creative-stage audit runs before any exclusion change when frequency rises with flat cold reach, then fatigue gets fixed at the real cause because too many product-aware or feature-led ads is usually the actual problem.

signal.check: Cold frequency is rising while cold reach stays flat, and the response under consideration is a new exclusion rather than a review of the creative mix by awareness stage.
