expected_effect.size: unknown; a healthy starting split is roughly 80% unaware and problem aware, 10% solution aware, 10% product and most aware

risk.note: Conflicts with fixing exclusions first; use this as the first move, not the only one.

prerequisites: Live ad library tagged by awareness stage
steps: Tag every live ad by awareness stage: unaware, problem, solution, product, most aware.
Compare the mix against a roughly 80/10/10 starting split.
If too many ads are product-aware or feature-led, brief more unaware and problem-aware creative.
Only look at exclusions afterward if frequency is still high.

test.method: Compare cold reach and frequency trend before and after rebalancing the creative mix.

title: Watch frequency and ROAS trend together on narrow-persona ads and brief a new concept when ROAS taper starts
hypothesis: If frequency and ROAS are tracked together weekly on narrow-persona ads, then a new concept gets briefed at the right moment because rising frequency paired with tapering ROAS is the signal to stop iterating.

signal.check: A narrow-persona ad's frequency is rising and its ROAS is tapering, but the response has been another small edit instead of a new concept brief.

risk.note: A monitoring and briefing habit, not a targeting change.

prerequisites: Ad-level frequency and ROAS trend by week
steps: Track weekly frequency and ROAS for narrow-persona ads.
Watch for the pattern of rising frequency paired with tapering ROAS.
When it appears, brief a genuinely new concept, not another small edit.
Launch the new concept in its own ad set.

test.method: Compare ROAS recovery after briefing a new concept versus after iterating on the same ad.
test.read_point: 2 to 4 weeks after the new concept launches.

title: Keep a creative pipeline running so the account's top ad's eventual fatigue does not stall spend
hypothesis: If a creative pipeline stays active even while one ad dominates, then spend never stalls when that ad fatigues because a next concept is already in test.

signal.check: The account has a single dominant ad and no other concept currently in active testing to replace it when it fatigues.

risk.note: A pipeline-planning habit, not a change to the current winner.

prerequisites: A production process that can brief new concepts regularly
steps: Check whether any concept besides the current dominant ad is in active testing.
If not, brief at least one new concept immediately.
Keep at least one concept in test at all times, regardless of how well the top ad is doing.
Review pipeline health monthly.

test.method: Track spend and ROAS in the weeks right after the dominant ad's ROAS eventually drops.

title: Ask 'where can cold spend grow' for prospecting and 'where can this shrink' for retargeting
hypothesis: If prospecting budget decisions ask where cold spend can grow while retargeting decisions ask where spend can shrink, then retargeting stops crowding out growth because it is treated as a support layer, not a growth line.

signal.check: Retargeting or cart-abandoner campaigns are being reviewed for growth potential in the same way prospecting campaigns are.

expected_effect.size: unknown; audits often find about 50% of spend on existing plus engaged, which is a mistake

risk.note: A framing rule for budget reviews, not an immediate spend cut.

steps: When reviewing prospecting campaigns, ask where cold spend can grow.
When reviewing retargeting and past-buyer campaigns, ask where spend can shrink instead.
Apply this question consistently across Meta, TikTok and Pinterest retargeting.
Escalate any retargeting campaign that keeps growing under this question.

test.method: Track retargeting share of total spend over 3 months after adopting this framing.

title: Skip a website-visitor retargeting campaign unless the engaged segment is starved of cold spend
hypothesis: If a website-visitor retargeting campaign only launches when the audience breakdown shows the engaged segment starved of spend from cold campaigns, then budget stops leaking into a redundant campaign for most accounts.

signal.check: A website-visitor retargeting campaign is running, or is being proposed, without first checking whether the engaged segment already gets meaningful spend and frequency from cold campaigns.

expected_effect.size: unknown; about 90% of accounts do not need this campaign

risk.note: Some accounts genuinely need it; check the data before cutting.

prerequisites: Audience segment breakdown with spend and frequency by segment
steps: Pull the audience segment breakdown for cold campaigns.
Check whether the engaged segment already gets meaningful spend and frequency from cold.
If yes, skip or pause the dedicated website-visitor retargeting campaign.
If the engaged segment is genuinely starved, keep or launch it, consolidated with no add-to-cart or checkout splits.

test.method: Compare account-wide CPA before and after pausing an unnecessary website-visitor campaign.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the change.

title: Size existing-customer ad budget in dollars and frequency, never as a percentage of spend
hypothesis: If existing-customer budget is set from customers times CPM divided by 1,000 times desired frequency, then retargeting spend stays sized to the actual customer file instead of drifting with a percentage of an unrelated cold budget.

signal.check: Existing-customer or retention ad budget is set as a percentage of total spend rather than calculated from customer count, CPM and target frequency.

expected_effect.size: unknown; example 50,000 customers x ($10 CPM / 1,000) x 2 desired monthly frequency = $1,000 a month

risk.note: Only run this when repeat purchase is genuinely expected for the category.

prerequisites: Customer file size
Retargeting CPM
Repeat purchase expectation for the category
steps: Confirm repeat purchase is expected for this category before running any existing-customer budget.
Calculate monthly budget as customers x (CPM / 1,000) x desired monthly frequency, keeping frequency below 7.
Set that as the fixed dollar budget instead of a percentage of total spend.
Re-derive the number whenever customer count or CPM changes meaningfully.

test.method: Compare existing-customer frequency and spend efficiency before and after switching to the dollar-based formula.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the change.

title: Hold all existing-customer spend in one dedicated campaign so it cannot bleed into cold
hypothesis: If existing-customer spend lives in exactly one dedicated campaign, then cold spend stops being contaminated because there is a single, auditable place where retention budget sits.

signal.check: Existing-customer or retargeting spend is spread across more than one campaign, or is not clearly separated from cold campaigns.

risk.note: A structural consolidation, not a spend change.

prerequisites: A defined existing-customer audience segment
steps: List every campaign currently targeting existing or engaged customers.
Consolidate them into one dedicated campaign.
Confirm no cold campaign includes existing customers.
Audit this monthly at the structure review.

test.method: Recheck the audience breakdown after consolidation to confirm existing customers show near 0% in cold.

title: Do not hyper-segment retargeting by funnel stage, warmth tier or page viewed
hypothesis: If retargeting stays consolidated instead of split by add-to-cart, checkout, page or warmth tier, then the CPM increase from hyper-segmentation stops eating the conversion-rate gain it was supposed to buy.

signal.check: Retargeting is split into many small ad sets by add-to-cart, checkout stage, page viewed or warmth tier.

risk.note: A consolidation, not a targeting removal; keep the retargeting audience, just merge the ad sets.

prerequisites: Current retargeting ad set list
steps: List all current retargeting ad sets and their split logic.
Merge ad sets that only differ by funnel stage, warmth tier or page viewed.
For fashion or multi-category stores, keep at most 2 ad sets: new arrivals and DPA.
Recheck CPM and CPA after consolidating.

test.method: Compare CPM and CPA before and after merging hyper-segmented retargeting ad sets.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the merge.

title: Retarget non-buyers with a different offer, proof or objection-handling ad, not the same ad louder
hypothesis: If non-buyers see a different offer, proof point or objection-handling ad instead of the same prospecting ad repeated, then retargeting converts better because repetition alone does not answer why they did not buy.

signal.check: Non-buyer retargeting shows the exact same ad used in cold prospecting, with no different offer, proof or objection handling.

risk.note: Requires more than one product or offer to rotate in.

prerequisites: More than one product, offer or proof point available
steps: List the objections or hesitations a non-buyer likely has.
Build at least one ad addressing an objection directly, with proof or risk reversal.
Build at least one ad offering a different product or bundle.
Rotate these into non-buyer retargeting instead of the original prospecting ad.

test.method: Compare conversion rate on non-buyer retargeting before and after adding varied creative.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the change.

title: Keep DPA out of the cold CBO in its own ad set, and cap its share of total spend
hypothesis: If DPA runs in its own ad set outside the cold CBO with a spend-share cap, then prospecting stops getting starved because DPA's easy wins are no longer competing directly with new-customer ads for the same budget.

signal.check: DPA ads run inside the same cold CBO as prospecting ads, or DPA's share of total spend is approaching 57% to 80% with no cap in place.

expected_effect.size: unknown; example 6 fashion brands at about 80% DPA share saw a 6-month decline

risk.note: Cutting DPA too hard without rebuilding prospecting first can also hurt revenue; rebuild top of funnel in parallel.

prerequisites: A defined existing-customer or DPA campaign separate from cold
steps: Move DPA into its own ad set inside the existing-customer campaign, not the cold CBO.
Track DPA's share of total account spend.
Set a cap, such as staying well under 57% to 70%, and alert if it is approached.
If DPA share is high and declining, rebuild top-of-funnel prospecting rather than cutting DPA alone.

test.method: Track DPA share of spend monthly and its trend over 6 months.

title: Read DPA on 7-day click or incremental attribution, never on its blended platform ROAS
hypothesis: If DPA is read on 7-day click or incremental attribution instead of its blended platform ROAS, then its real contribution becomes visible because DPA ROAS largely mirrors top-of-funnel spend rather than its own performance.

signal.check: DPA's blended ROAS is being used to justify keeping or growing it, without checking its 7-day-click or incremental number.

expected_effect.size: unknown; example furniture DPA shown at 7x blended versus 1.9x on 7-day click or incremental

risk.note: Never cut prospecting because DPA looks strong on a blended number; that is the death-spiral pattern.

prerequisites: Compare-attribution-settings column available for the DPA campaign
steps: Pull DPA's blended ROAS and its 7-day-click or incremental ROAS side by side.
Use the tighter number as the true read of DPA's contribution.
Never cut prospecting spend to protect a DPA campaign that only looks strong on blended ROAS.
Report both numbers whenever DPA performance is discussed.

test.method: Track the gap between DPA's blended and tightened ROAS monthly.

title: Time win-back or reminder ads to land just before a customer's typical reorder date
hypothesis: If win-back or reminder ads are timed to a customer's typical reorder date instead of a fixed retargeting schedule, then repeat purchase improves because the message arrives when the customer is actually about to run out.

signal.check: Existing-customer retargeting for a repeat-purchase category runs on a fixed schedule rather than being timed to each customer's expected reorder date.

risk.note: No library source gives a reminder-timing rule; verify against the brand's own repurchase-cycle data.

prerequisites: Repurchase cycle length by product or customer
steps: Calculate the typical repurchase cycle for the product or customer segment.
Build a reminder or win-back audience timed to trigger just before that date.
Route a dedicated ad to that audience instead of the generic retargeting schedule.
Track repeat purchase rate for customers who saw the timed reminder versus those who did not.

test.method: Compare repeat purchase rate for the timed-reminder group against a matched control group.

title: For high-AOV considered purchases, run a longer nurture ladder before a same-day retargeting push
hypothesis: If high-AOV, slow-purchase-cycle categories get a nurture ladder of proof, financing and objection handling before a same-day retargeting push, then conversion improves because a considered buyer is not rushed the way an impulse buyer would be.

signal.check: A high-AOV, considered-purchase category retargets non-buyers with the same same-day push used for low-consideration products, with no staged proof, financing or objection-handling sequence.

risk.note: No library source gives a nurture-ladder template for this category type; verify against the brand's own sales cycle data.

prerequisites: A defined purchase cycle length for the category
steps: Map the typical decision stages for the high-AOV purchase.
Build a sequence: proof and social validation first, then financing or EMI messaging, then objection handling.
Delay the same-day, urgency-style retargeting push until later in the sequence.
Track conversion rate against the old same-day-push approach.

test.method: Compare conversion rate and time-to-purchase for buyers on the nurture ladder versus the old approach.

title: State the return or exchange policy clearly in non-buyer retargeting and objection-handling ads
hypothesis: If the return or exchange policy is stated clearly in non-buyer retargeting and objection ads, then hesitant buyers convert more because a clear policy reads as a trust signal, not just a logistics note.

signal.check: Non-buyer retargeting and objection-handling ads make no mention of the return or exchange policy, especially for higher-consideration or higher-AOV products.

risk.note: No library source treats return policy as a shopper-facing trust signal; every mention found was about ROAS or logistics.

prerequisites: A clear, accurate return or exchange policy to state
steps: Pull the store's actual return or exchange policy.
Write a short, plain version of it for ad copy.
Add it to non-buyer retargeting and objection-handling ads, especially for higher-AOV products.
Check it matches the policy shown on the product page.

test.method: Compare conversion rate on non-buyer retargeting ads with and without the policy line.

title: Turn off flexible or dynamic-crop ads on catalogue and product ads
hypothesis: If flexible or dynamic-crop ads stay off on catalogue and product ads, then shoppers never see a cropped or mismatched product photo they did not order, because the exact asset that drove results stays readable too.

signal.check: Flexible or dynamic-crop ads are turned on for catalogue or product ads, so the exact image or crop a shopper saw cannot be confirmed.

risk.note: Check the current in-platform name for this setting before turning it off.

prerequisites: Access to ad-level creative settings
steps: Open the creative settings for catalogue and product ads.
Turn off flexible or dynamic-crop ads.
Recheck recently launched ads, since this setting can default back on.
Confirm the exact approved image is what serves.

test.method: Audit a sample of live product ads monthly for flexible or crop settings creeping back on.

title: Turn off Advantage+ creative edits on every product ad
hypothesis: If Advantage+ creative edits stay off on every product ad, then an automatic overlay can never misstate a product's size, material or price, because the approved creative is what actually serves.

signal.check: Advantage+ creative optimisations are turned on for product ads, especially apparel or jewellery, where an automatic overlay could misstate size, material or price.

risk.note: Recheck recently launched ads, since this setting can default back on.

prerequisites: Access to advertiser and ad-level creative settings
steps: Open advertiser settings and the creative sub-dropdown for automated rules.
Turn off Advantage+ creative optimisations account-wide.
Turn off the same setting per ad on every launch.
Recheck settings on recently launched ads every 2 weeks.

test.method: Audit a sample of recently launched ads every 2 weeks for the setting turning back on.

title: Define new, engaged and existing audience segments and check the customer sync regularly
hypothesis: If new, engaged and existing audience segments are defined and their customer sync is checked on a schedule, then frequency and breakdown reads stop being meaningless because the underlying sync from Klaviyo or another source keeps working.

signal.check: Audience segments are not defined in advertiser settings, or the customer file sync has not been checked recently.

risk.note: A broken sync silently lets existing customers get served as new; check this before trusting any breakdown.

prerequisites: A customer file source, such as Klaviyo
steps: Define new, engaged and existing segments in advertiser settings.
Confirm the customer file sync source and its last successful sync date.
Set a recurring calendar check for the sync, such as monthly.
Re-verify the audience breakdown after any sync fix.

test.method: Check the sync status and re-verify the audience breakdown monthly.

title: Check attribution window and audience segment before trusting a too-good ROAS number
hypothesis: If any standout ROAS is checked against its attribution window and audience segment before being trusted, then false winners get caught early because a great number often comes from view-through credit or existing-customer mix.

signal.check: A campaign, ad set or ad shows a ROAS far above the rest of the account and is about to be scaled or praised without checking its attribution setting and audience segment first.

risk.note: A verification step before any scale decision, not a change to the ad itself.

prerequisites: Compare-attribution-settings and audience-segment breakdown columns
steps: Whenever a standout ROAS appears, pull its attribution window setting.
Pull the audience segment breakdown for the same ad or ad set.
Check whether the number holds under 7-day click and with existing customers excluded.
Only treat it as a real winner if it holds under both checks.

test.method: Track how many standout numbers survive this check versus how many turn out to be inflated.

title: Plan extra ad pages before hitting the live-ad-per-page cap
hypothesis: If duplicate brand pages, partnership pages and regional pages are planned ahead of the live-ad cap, then high creative volume never gets blocked because there is always page headroom to publish new ads.

signal.check: Live ads per page are approaching the platform's per-page cap with no additional pages planned, especially for high-volume or multi-country accounts.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the cap is roughly 300 to 500 live ads per page

risk.note: Check the current cap and page-creation rules before building extra pages.

prerequisites: High creative volume or a multi-country account
steps: Check current live ads per page against the platform cap.
If approaching the cap, build duplicate brand pages, partnership pages, or regional pages.
Route new ad volume to the pages with headroom.
Recheck page headroom monthly for high-volume accounts.

test.method: Track live ads per page monthly against the cap.

title: Run every audit as a ranked 90-day roadmap naming one constraint, not a list of screenshots
hypothesis: If every audit ends in one named constraint and a ranked 90-day roadmap instead of a list of settings errors, then the audit actually gets acted on because the founder knows exactly what to fix first.

signal.check: A recent or planned audit produces a long list of individual settings issues with no single named constraint or ranked order of fixes.

risk.note: Refuse to audit on platform data alone; get backend access first.

prerequisites: Backend order and margin data access
steps: Get backend access to orders, margin and platform data before starting.
Identify the single biggest constraint on profitable growth.
Rank every proposed fix by commercial impact into a 90-day roadmap.
Deliver the roadmap, not a raw list of settings findings.

test.method: Track how many roadmap items actually get implemented within 90 days.

title: Start every audit at store and new-customer revenue, not the ad platform
hypothesis: If every audit starts at store revenue and new-customer revenue instead of the ad platform, then the real constraint gets found faster because platform numbers cannot see refunds, COGS or repeat buyers.

signal.check: An audit is starting from Ads Manager or TikTok Ads Manager data before pulling Shopify revenue, new-customer revenue and CAC.

risk.note: A sequencing rule for how an audit begins.

prerequisites: Shopify or store revenue data
New-customer revenue and CAC
steps: Pull Shopify revenue, new-customer revenue and CAC first.
Name the likely problem type from that view before opening the ad platform.
Then find which platform the problem lives on.
Only then drill into campaigns, ad sets and ads.
Review the whole account at once, not one campaign at a time.

test.method: Compare the constraint named from store-first audits versus platform-first audits over several accounts.

title: Run the full structure review checklist at every audit, not a partial check
hypothesis: If every audit runs the same structure checklist (campaign purpose, 30-day frequency by segment, attribution consistency, a real testing structure, and settings and naming errors), then structure problems stop being missed because the same list gets checked every time.

signal.check: An audit is being run without a written checklist covering campaign purpose, frequency by segment, attribution consistency, testing structure, and settings and naming errors.

expected_effect.size: unknown; often about half of a legacy account's campaigns cannot be defended

risk.note: Naming that does not match settings is usually the most common finding.

prerequisites: List of all campaigns with a written one-line purpose
steps: List every campaign with its one-line defendable purpose; cut or merge what fails.
Check 30-day frequency by segment.
Check attribution consistency across campaigns.
Confirm a methodical testing structure exists.
Check settings errors: segments not defined, app rewards placement, legacy targeting, missing exclusions, names that lie.

test.method: Score the structure against this checklist before and after fixes.

title: Run the creative review in a fixed order: volume, then diversity, then quality
hypothesis: If creative gets reviewed in the fixed order of volume, then diversity, then quality, then the one real bottleneck gets found because each stage rules out a simpler explanation before moving to a harder one.

signal.check: A creative review jumps straight to judging ad quality without first checking whether volume and concept diversity are anywhere near the account's band.

risk.note: Quality has no fixed checklist in the source material; hand that stage to the creative team's own review process.

prerequisites: New ads per month and concept counts for the period
steps: Check volume: new ads per month against monthly spend divided by $1,000.
If volume is fine, check diversity: total concepts and winning concepts against the spend-tier band.
If diversity is fine, review creative quality directly, reading scripts and watching ads with direct-response judgment.
Name exactly one bottleneck from this order, not all three at once.

test.method: Track which of the three stages was named as the bottleneck across successive audits.

title: Validate any structure against 4 fixed questions before shipping it
hypothesis: If every proposed structure change is checked against 4 fixed questions before going live, then bad rebuilds get caught early because any single 'no' sends the plan back for revision.

signal.check: A new or restructured account plan is about to launch without checking readable data, commercial fit, spend-tier and creative-throughput fit, and support-layer sizing.

risk.note: A pre-launch gate, not a change after the fact.

prerequisites: A drafted structure plan
steps: Ask: is the data readable, so a decide-wait-decide loop works.
Ask: does the structure match how the business actually makes money.
Ask: is it right for the spend tier and creative throughput.
Ask: are support layers like retargeting sized to real retention.
Any 'no' sends the plan back to be rebuilt before launch.

test.method: Track how many launched structures later needed a rebuild, before and after using this gate.

title: Build a normalized contribution-margin P&L monthly to see whether scaling actually pays
hypothesis: If a normalized contribution-margin P&L runs monthly (revenue minus refunds and discounts, plus shipping collected, minus COGS, fulfilment, fees and marketing), then a scale-up that quietly loses money gets caught because margin is tracked, not assumed.

signal.check: The account has no normalized contribution-margin P&L, so nobody can say whether contribution margin fell as ad spend rose.

risk.note: Requires accurate COGS, fulfilment and fee data; garbage inputs give a false sense of accuracy.

prerequisites: Gross revenue, refunds, discounts, shipping collected, COGS, fulfilment cost, platform fees, marketing spend
steps: Pull gross revenue, refunds and discounts for the month.
Add shipping collected and subtract COGS, fulfilment cost and platform fees.
Subtract marketing spend to get contribution margin.
Track whether contribution margin rose or fell as ad spend rose.

test.method: Compare contribution margin trend against ad spend trend over the last 6 months.

title: Build GP cohort growth curves at day 90, 180 and 365 to set the right CAC tolerance
hypothesis: If gross profit cohort growth is charted at day 90, 180 and 365, then the CAC tolerance gets set correctly because strong retention can justify a lower first-order GP-to-CAC band and weak retention needs a higher one.

signal.check: The GP-to-CAC band is being applied the same way regardless of how strong or weak the store's retention curve actually is.

risk.note: Needs enough order history to build a reliable cohort curve.

prerequisites: Orders with customer id and date, 12+ months of history
steps: Build cohorts by first-purchase month.
Track cumulative gross profit per cohort at day 90, 180 and 365.
Compare cohort strength against category benchmarks if available.
Adjust the GP-to-CAC scale-ceiling band up or down based on how strong the curve is.

test.method: Recheck the cohort curve and adjusted CAC tolerance every 6 months.

title: Run a monthly platform-ROAS-versus-aMER reconciliation using the attribution comparison columns
hypothesis: If platform ROAS and acquisition MER get reconciled every month using the attribution comparison columns, then the account always knows which number to trust because the gap and its likely cause are checked on a fixed schedule, not only when something looks wrong.

signal.check: Platform ROAS and acquisition MER are compared only occasionally or only when a number looks suspicious, not on a fixed monthly schedule.

expected_effect.size: unknown; example gap is aMER 3x to 7x versus platform ROAS as high as 17x

risk.note: A recurring process, not a one-time fix.

prerequisites: Monthly new-customer revenue and ad spend by platform
Compare-attribution-settings columns
steps: Calculate aMER for the month from store data.
Put each platform's account ROAS beside it.
Add the compare-attribution-settings columns on Meta: 7-day click, 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view, incremental.
Choose to switch settings to match aMER, or keep settings and always judge on the comparison column.

test.method: Track the platform-ROAS-to-aMER gap every month and flag any month it widens.

title: Complete the full TikTok account setup before spending any budget
hypothesis: If business info, documents, payment methods, audience controls and brand safety are all complete before the first dollar spends, then TikTok launches do not stall on account health issues mid-flight.

signal.check: A new TikTok ad account is about to spend without documents, a backup payment method, audience controls or brand safety hub fully set up.

risk.note: Business Center is required for any team of more than one user; use 2-step auth and an allowed email domain.

prerequisites: Business documents
A card on file plus a backup payment method
steps: Complete business info and upload required documents.
Add a card on file, turn on automatic payments, and add a backup payment method.
Set audience controls and configure the brand safety hub with standard inventory.
Confirm account health reads good or excellent before spending.

test.method: Check account health status right before the first campaign launches.

title: Test every TikTok pixel event before launch and stop if purchase or add to cart does not fire
hypothesis: If every pixel event is tested with Pixel Helper or Test Events before launch, then wasted spend never happens because a campaign never runs on an untracked purchase or add-to-cart event.

signal.check: A TikTok Sales campaign is about to launch and page view, view content, add to cart, initiate checkout and complete payment have not all been tested.

risk.note: If purchase or add to cart does not fire, stop and fix the pixel before spending.

prerequisites: TikTok pixel installed via the official Shopify app
steps: Install the pixel through the official TikTok for Shopify app.
Open Pixel Helper or Test Events.
Test page view, view content, add to cart, initiate checkout and complete payment.
Stop and fix the install if purchase or add to cart does not fire.

test.method: Recheck all 5 events fire correctly right before every new campaign launch.

title: Launch the first TikTok campaign as a manual Sales campaign with the catalog off
hypothesis: If the first TikTok campaign runs as a manual Sales campaign to a website with the catalog off, then the pixel gets credit for real checkouts because delivery is not diluted by browsing a synced catalogue.

signal.check: A first TikTok in-feed campaign is being set up as Smart+ or with the catalog on, rather than manual with the catalog off.

risk.note: Smart+ can be tested later as a parallel campaign once the manual structure is proven.

prerequisites: Working pixel with Complete Payment event
steps: Create the campaign with objective Sales, destination Website.
Choose Manual, not Smart+.
Turn the catalog off.
Name the campaign product plus objective plus date.

test.method: Compare CPA between the manual catalog-off campaign and any later Smart+ test.

title: Set the first TikTok ad group to broad targeting, Complete Payment optimisation, no target CPA
hypothesis: If the first TikTok ad group targets broad with Complete Payment optimisation and no target CPA, then the account gets a clean read because nothing narrows delivery before the algorithm has any data.

signal.check: A new TikTok ad group launches with narrow interests, a target CPA set, or dayparting instead of broad targeting and no target CPA.

risk.note: Read the placement breakdown after about a week and opt out of weak placements.

prerequisites: Working pixel with Complete Payment event
steps: Set optimisation to website conversion, event Complete Payment.
Set placements to TikTok only, or automatic with a placement read after 1 week.
Target broad: country, language, 18+, all spending power, all income, all devices.
Leave target CPA blank and use a continuous schedule.

test.method: Read the placement breakdown after 1 week and compare CPA to a matched interest-targeted ad group.

title: Keep TikTok interests broad: 2 to 5 parent categories, never 15 to 20 stacked interests
hypothesis: If any TikTok interest ad group uses only 2 to 5 broad parent categories instead of 15 to 20 stacked interests, then CPA stays lower because over-stacking interests has been shown to raise cost per result sharply.

signal.check: A TikTok interest ad group is stacking 15 or more specific interests instead of 2 to 5 broad parent categories.

expected_effect.size: one case showed 15+ interests giving CPA above 100 versus 34 to 41 with 1 broad category

risk.note: Test interests as a second ad group beside the broad one, using the same ads.

prerequisites: A working broad ad group already running
steps: Build a second ad group with the same ads as the broad one.
Add 2 to 5 broad parent-category interests, or a purchaser lookalike.
Never stack 15 to 20 specific interests together.
Compare CPA against the broad ad group; keep broad if there is no clear difference.

test.method: Compare CPA between the broad and interest ad groups after the first test window.
test.read_point: After the first test window (see TikTok first-test idea).

title: Set TikTok daily budget at the greater of $50 or 2x current CPA per ad group
hypothesis: If TikTok ad group budgets are set to the greater of $50 a day or 2 times current CPA, then ad groups collect enough data to be read because they are never starved below the platform's practical learning floor.

signal.check: A TikTok ad group is running at the $20 platform minimum or below 2x current CPA, with no clear reason for the low floor.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2x CPA buys about 14 results in 7 days, short of TikTok's 25-in-7 learning exit

risk.note: Raise toward about 3.6x CPA a day only if hitting the 25-in-7 learning read genuinely matters.

prerequisites: Current CPA, or an allowable CPA target if CPA is unknown
steps: Calculate 2x current CPA, or use about $50 a day if CPA is unknown.
Set the ad group's daily budget to the greater of that number or $50.
Raise toward about 3.6x CPA a day if the 25-in-7 learning read matters and the brand's CPA supports it.
Never set an ad group below the $20 platform floor.

test.method: Track ad group budget against this floor and the resulting learning status after 7 days.

title: Grow TikTok structure with budget: broad ad group first, then an interest ad group, cap at 4 ad groups
hypothesis: If TikTok structure starts with one broad ad group and adds an interest ad group only as budget grows, capped at about 4 ad groups per campaign, then the account avoids spreading thin budget across too many small tests.

signal.check: A TikTok campaign already has more than about 4 ad groups, or an interest ad group was added before the broad ad group had a fair read.

risk.note: Build all planned ads in the first ad group before duplicating into a second.

prerequisites: A broad ad group already tested
steps: Start with 1 Prospecting campaign and 1 broad ad group with 3 ads.
Add an interest ad group with the same 3 to 5 ads once the broad group has a read.
Cap the campaign at no more than 4 ad groups.
Move a confirmed winner into its own CBO scaling campaign.

test.method: Track CPA and read confidence as ad groups are added under this cap.
test.read_point: After each ad group's read window.

title: Run the TikTok first test as 2 ad groups x 3 creatives x $50 a day x 3 to 4 days
hypothesis: If the first TikTok test runs as 2 ad groups of 3 very different creatives at $50 a day for 3 to 4 days, then the account gets a real first read because it hits about $300 to $400 of spend before any ad is touched.

signal.check: A first TikTok test launches with fewer than 3 very different creatives per ad group, under $50 a day, or gets touched before 1,000 impressions or $50 of spend per ad.

expected_effect.size: about $300 to $400 total for the first test

risk.note: Do not touch anything before $50 spend or 1,000 impressions per ad.

prerequisites: 3 or more very different creatives ready
steps: Build 2 ad groups with 3 very different creatives each.
Set each ad group's budget to at least $50 a day.
Run for 3 to 4 days without touching the ads.
Read at 24 hours on soft metrics and at 3 days on cost metrics.

test.method: Read CTR, watch time and CPM at 24 hours, then CPC, cost per add to cart and CPA at 3 days.
test.read_point: At 24 hours and again at 3 days.

title: Read the TikTok first test at 24 hours on soft metrics and at 3 days on cost metrics, then cut the bottom half
hypothesis: If the first TikTok test is read at 24 hours on CTR, watch time and CPM, then again at 3 days on CPC, cost per add-to-cart and CPA, then weak creative and weak audiences get told apart because each metric flags a different problem.

signal.check: TikTok test ads are being judged on cost metrics alone at 24 hours, before they have enough spend, or never checked against the soft-metric thresholds at all.

expected_effect.size: CTR above 1% good, below 1% a creative problem; watch time above 25% good, below 20% a hook problem; CPM under $15 good, above $20 an audience problem

risk.note: US heuristics and undated; replace the cost thresholds with the brand's own allowable CPA.

prerequisites: Each ad has at least $50 spend or 1,000 impressions
steps: At 24 hours, read CTR, watch time and CPM against the soft-metric thresholds.
Diagnose the likely cause: creative, hook or audience.
At 3 days, read CPC, cost per add to cart and cost per purchase against the brand's own allowable CPA.
Kill the bottom 50% of ads by the brand's cost metric and brief new variations of the winners.

test.method: Track how often the 24-hour diagnosis (creative, hook, audience) matches the 3-day cost result.

title: Seed TikTok lookalikes from purchasers or visitors instead of targeting them directly
hypothesis: If TikTok lookalikes are seeded from purchasers or 180-day visitors instead of targeting the custom audience directly, then prospecting reaches new people because the seed audience feeds a wider lookalike pool.

signal.check: A TikTok prospecting ad group targets a custom audience of purchasers or visitors directly, instead of using it as a lookalike seed.

risk.note: Size the lookalike balanced for large countries and broad for small ones.

prerequisites: A custom audience of purchasers or site visitors
steps: Build a custom audience from purchasers, or 30 to 180-day visitors.
Use it as the seed for a lookalike audience, not as direct targeting.
Size the lookalike balanced for large countries, broad for small countries.
Keep this lookalike platform-specific; do not assume it behaves like a Meta lookalike.

test.method: Compare CPA on the lookalike ad group versus the broad ad group over the same window.

title: Move a winning TikTok creative into its own CBO scaling campaign, keep testing in the manual campaign
hypothesis: If a winning TikTok creative moves into its own CBO scaling campaign while the manual campaign keeps testing, then the winner scales cleanly because it is no longer competing with new, unproven ads for the same ad group's budget.

signal.check: A winning TikTok ad is still sitting in the same manual testing ad group as new, unproven creative.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no TikTok-specific step size or pacing is given, so borrow the Meta pacing rule

risk.note: Borrow Meta's pacing (about 20% daily steps) since TikTok sources give no step size of their own.

prerequisites: A confirmed winning TikTok ad
steps: Confirm the ad is a clear winner over a full read window.
Move it into a separate CBO scaling campaign.
Keep testing new creative in the original manual campaign.
Pace budget increases in the scaling campaign using the same steps as the Meta scaling idea.

test.method: Compare CPA and spend growth in the scaling campaign against the original ad group's plateau.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the move.

title: Post organically first, wait 5 to 7 days, then Spark the winning posts
hypothesis: If content posts organically first and only the winners from the first 5 to 7 days get turned into Spark Ads, then ad spend goes behind content that has already proven it can perform.

signal.check: Content is being boosted into Spark Ads immediately after posting, without an organic-first window to see which posts perform.

expected_effect.size: unknown; Spark Ads are said to carry higher CTR and lower CPA than a cold-launched ad

risk.note: A post that is going to take off usually shows within about 2 days.

prerequisites: 3 or more organic posts to test
steps: Post 3 or more videos organically, own account or creator accounts.
Wait 5 to 7 days before deciding.
Pick winners by sales, follows or engagement.
Boost the top 10% to 30% of a larger batch into Spark Ads.

test.method: Compare CTR and CPA on Spark Ads sourced from proven organic winners versus ads boosted immediately.

title: Get a 365-day authorization code from creators before Sparking their content
hypothesis: If a 365-day ad authorization code is collected from every creator before their post is Sparked, then the ad can keep running and be edited without a mid-flight authorization lapse.

signal.check: A creator's post is being Sparked without a stored, 365-day authorization code on file.

risk.note: A short or missing authorization can force a Sparked ad to stop delivering mid-test.

prerequisites: A creator willing to share their post for ads
steps: Ask the creator for an ad authorization code from their post settings.
Confirm the duration is set to 365 days.
Store the code and the post link together.
Paste the code under add post when building the Spark ad.

test.method: Track how many Sparked ads stop delivering due to authorization issues before and after this process.

title: Run TikTok Search with 20 to 50 keywords, phrase match, and add negatives regularly
hypothesis: If TikTok Search runs with 20 to 50 keywords on phrase match and gets negative keywords added regularly, then search spend stays efficient because irrelevant terms get cut before they waste budget.

signal.check: TikTok Search is running with automated keywords on, far fewer than 20 keywords, or no negative-keyword review process.

risk.note: Skip Search entirely if keyword volume for the product is negligible.

prerequisites: A working pixel with Complete Payment event
steps: Pull 20 to 50 relevant keywords from Keyword Planner, starting with low competition.
Set match type to phrase and turn automated keywords off at launch.
Launch the Search campaign with the saved keyword plan.
Review search terms after a couple of days and add negatives regularly.

test.method: Track CPA and wasted spend on irrelevant search terms before and after the negative-keyword review habit.

title: Set up TikTok Shop in Seller Center with complete listings before selling through it
hypothesis: If every red-starred Seller Center field is complete and listings read good or better before selling, then TikTok Shop avoids early rejections and poor discovery from an incomplete storefront.

signal.check: TikTok Shop is going live with incomplete Seller Center fields, unresolved restricted-category flags, or listings graded below good.

risk.note: Market availability for TikTok Shop and GMV Max should be checked before planning around them.

prerequisites: Same email as Shopify
Business documents for Seller Center
steps: Set up Seller Center with the same email as Shopify and complete business documents.
Connect via the official TikTok for Shopify app and fill every red-starred field.
Check restricted categories and fix any listing below good quality.
Connect Shop to Business Center and the TikTok profile before promoting it.

test.method: Check listing quality scores and Shop visibility in TikTok search after setup.

title: Structure TikTok affiliate commissions with open collabs for volume and targeted collabs for key partners
hypothesis: If open collaboration commissions cover general volume and targeted collaboration rates go to selected partners, then the affiliate program grows without overpaying every random creator the same rate as a proven one.

signal.check: The TikTok affiliate program pays one flat rate to every creator with no open-versus-targeted split or requester screening.

expected_effect.size: unknown; open commission example about 20%, shop-ads commission around 5%

risk.note: Shop-ads commission runs lower than standard because the brand is also paying for the ads themselves.

prerequisites: TikTok Shop live with products connected
steps: Set an open collaboration commission for general creators, such as around 20%.
Set follower and GMV thresholds for free product samples.
Offer targeted collaboration with custom rates to strong partners.
Review requesters by post rate and 30-day GMV before approving them.

test.method: Track affiliate-driven GMV and creator quality after adding the open-versus-targeted split.

title: Launch GMV Max on the top 20% of SKUs with an ROI target above break-even
lever: GMV Max SKU and ROI setup
hypothesis: If GMV Max starts with only the top 20% of SKUs by past orders and an ROI target set above break-even, then automated spend concentrates on proven sellers instead of chasing every SKU at an unprofitable target.

signal.check: GMV Max is running with all SKUs selected or with the ROI target left at TikTok's default suggestion, which is often below break-even.

expected_effect.size: unknown; demo ROI targets ranged 1.2 to 2.2, described as TikTok's suggestion plus 1

risk.note: Lower the ROI target one step only if there are no impressions after a few days.

prerequisites: Historical order data by SKU
A known break-even ROAS
steps: Rank SKUs by historical orders and select the top 20%.
Set the ROI target above the brand's own break-even ROAS, not TikTok's default suggestion.
Cap special promotion days at 50% and a 1x limit.
Turn on auto-select creative and boost strong videos at a $10 a day minimum on top of budget.

test.method: Track delivery status and ROI against break-even for the first week, adjusting the target if nothing delivers.

title: Build TikTok retargeting from site visitors and product viewers, excluding recent buyers
hypothesis: If TikTok retargeting targets site visitors and product-page viewers while excluding recent buyers, then spend chases shoppers who are still deciding instead of repeat buyers who already converted.

signal.check: TikTok retargeting targets all site visitors with no exclusion for buyers in the same window, or audience expansion is left on.

risk.note: New custom audiences take about 24 hours to populate before they can be used.

prerequisites: TikTok pixel with page view and purchase events working
steps: Build a custom audience of page view or view content visitors from the last 30 days.
Exclude purchasers from the last 30 days.
Turn off audience expansion.
Grow the tiers as budget allows: 7-day non-buyers, 30-day add-to-cart, then re-engagement content viewers.

test.method: Compare CPA and reach on the exclusion-built audience versus an unfiltered visitor audience.

title: Before dropping interests or lookalikes entirely, run one controlled 7-day broad-vs-stack test
hypothesis: If a 7-day same-creative broad-versus-interest-stack test runs with a stated minimum spend before interests are dropped for good, then the decision is based on this account's own data instead of a general claim that interests are dead.

signal.check: Interests or lookalikes are being removed, or kept, based on a general claim rather than a same-creative controlled test in this account.

risk.note: A time-boxed test, not a permanent targeting commitment either way.

prerequisites: A test-sizing method already in place
steps: Pick one concept with proven creative.
Launch it broad in one ad set and stacked with interests in a matched ad set, same creative in both.
State a minimum spend and conversion count before launch.
Run for 7 days and use the result to decide, not a general claim.

test.method: Compare CPA and conversion count between the broad and stacked ad sets after 7 days.

title: Name ad-set forks with the same concept fields plus launch date so performance can be tracked across forks
hypothesis: If every fork of a winning ad set keeps the same concept fields in its name with only the launch date changing, then a concept's total performance stays trackable because filtering by concept name pulls every fork together.

signal.check: A concept has been forked into several ad sets over time and the forks do not share a consistent concept name, making it hard to filter and sum the concept's total performance.

risk.note: A naming discipline applied at the moment of forking, not a retroactive rename requirement.

prerequisites: The account's naming convention (persona, angle, offer, content type, launch date)
steps: When forking a winning ad set, copy its persona, angle and offer fields exactly.
Change only the content type or launch date field in the new fork's name.
Filter by the shared concept fields to see total performance across all forks.
Apply this every time a new fork is created.

test.method: Check whether concept-level performance can be pulled correctly by filtering ad set names.

title: Track ad format as a spend-share signal inside concept ad sets, not as a separate ad set split
hypothesis: If image, video and DPA performance is read as a spend-share signal inside each concept ad set instead of split into separate format ad sets, then format insight is gathered without adding structure that only new, small accounts need.

signal.check: Format-based ad sets (image, video, DPA in separate ad sets) exist above small new-account spend, or format performance is not being read from spend share inside concept ad sets.

risk.note: Format ad sets are only appropriate for new accounts under about $10,000 a month.

prerequisites: Concept ad sets already running with mixed formats
steps: Check whether any format-only ad sets exist above about $10,000 a month spend.
If so, merge the formats back into their shared concept ad set.
Read format performance as spend share inside the concept ad set instead.
Use that read only to brief creative, not to move budget.

test.method: Compare CPA and creative-team briefing quality before and after merging format-only ad sets.

title: Watch per-ad video retention curves and fix drops at the product intro or call to action
hypothesis: If per-ad video retention curves are checked for sharp drops at the product intro or call to action, then that specific moment in the edit gets smoothed because a gradual decline is normal but a cliff at one point is not.

signal.check: A video ad's retention curve shows a sharp drop at a specific point, such as the product reveal or the call to action, and no one has flagged it for an edit.

risk.note: Requires access to per-ad video retention data in the platform.

prerequisites: Per-ad video retention curve data
steps: Pull the retention curve for the ad.
Look for a sharp drop rather than a gradual decline.
Identify what happens on screen at that timestamp, often the product intro or the call to action.
Re-edit that section to smooth the transition and re-test.

test.method: Compare the retention curve and hold rate before and after the re-edit.
test.read_point: 1 full read window after the re-edit.

title: Match TikTok video specs to platform requirements before upload to avoid rejection or weak delivery
hypothesis: If every TikTok video is exported to the platform's spec (9:16, 1080 by 1920, MP4, H.264, under the size limit) before upload, then ads stop getting rejected or delivered poorly for a fixable technical reason.

signal.check: A TikTok ad upload is rejected, or delivers poorly, and the video does not match the current 9:16, resolution, format or file-size spec.

risk.note: Check the current spec before every batch upload, since platform requirements change.

prerequisites: Video export settings control
steps: Check TikTok's current video spec before exporting.
Confirm the file is under the current size limit.
Re-export and re-check before uploading if the first attempt is rejected.

test.method: Track rejection rate and delivery status for spec-checked uploads versus prior uploads.
